entries.6.1: 'Assailed by them, the gods and the sages rich in penance, tormented by fear, went for refuge to Maheshvara, the god of gods —
entries.6.2: 'to the maker of the world's creation and its ending, the unborn, whose form is unmanifest, the support of all the worlds, the supreme teacher who is to be worshipped.
entries.6.3: 'Coming to the foe of Kama, the destroyer of the three cities, the three-eyed one, the gods spoke with joined palms, their voices faltering with fear.
entries.6.4: '"Lord, overseer of creatures, all beings are oppressed by the sons of Sukesha, who are made insolent by the Grandsire's boon and afflict us as enemies do.
entries.6.5: '"Our hermitages, which should be places of refuge, have been made no refuge at all. They cast the gods out of heaven and sport there in heaven as though they were gods.
entries.6.6: '"'I am Vishnu, I am Rudra, I am Brahma, I am the king of the gods; I am Yama and Varuna, I am the moon and I am the sun as well' —
entries.6.7: '"so say the rakshasas Mali, Sumali and Malyavan, exulting in battle, and those who go before them. Therefore, god, you should grant safety to us who are afflicted with fear.
entries.6.8: '"Take on your terrible form and destroy these thorns in the side of the gods."
entries.6.9: 'Being addressed thus by all the gods, the lord of the matted hair, dark and red, having still some regard for Sukesha, spoke to the hosts of the gods.
entries.6.10: '"I shall not slay them, gods, for they may not be slain by me. But I shall give you counsel by which they will be destroyed.
entries.6.11: '"Take up this very endeavour, great sages, and go for refuge to Vishnu. That lord will slay them."
entries.6.12: 'Then, greeting Maheshvara with cries of victory, they came into Vishnu's presence, tormented by fear of the night-rangers.
entries.6.13: 'Bowing to the god who bears the conch and the discus and honouring him greatly, they spoke in agitation about the sons of Sukesha.
entries.6.14: '"God, by the three sons of Sukesha, who are like the threefold sacrificial fire, our stations have been overrun and taken from us by the power of a boon.
entries.6.15: '"There is a city named Lanka, hard to assail, standing on the peak of Trikuta. Established there, those night-rangers oppress us all.
entries.6.16: '"Therefore, slayer of Madhu, destroy them for our good. We have come to you for refuge; be our recourse, lord of the gods.
entries.6.17: '"Send their lotus-faces, severed by your discus, to Yama. In our fears there is no other giver of safety to us but you.
entries.6.18: '"Dispel our fear, god, as the sun dispels the mist — the fear of those wicked rakshasas in battle, insolent with pride, and of all who follow them."
entries.6.19: 'Being addressed thus by the gods, Janardana, god of gods, who gives fear to his enemies, granted them safety and said:
entries.6.20: '"I know the rakshasa Sukesha, made proud by Ishana's boon; and I know those sons of his, of whom Malyavan is the eldest.
entries.6.21: '"In my wrath I shall destroy those lowest of rakshasas, who have overstepped all bounds. Be free of your fever, gods."
entries.6.22: 'Being addressed thus by Vishnu the mighty, all those gods went gladly to their dwellings, praising Janardana.
entries.6.23: 'But the night-ranger Malyavan, hearing of the gods' endeavour, spoke these words to his two brave brothers.
entries.6.24: '"The immortals and the sages, it seems, went together to Shankara and, seeking our destruction, spoke these words:
entries.6.25: '"'God, the sons of Sukesha, made insolent by the power of a boon, oppress us at every step, arrogant and dreadful of form.
entries.6.26: '"'We are overcome by the rakshasas, Prajapati, and we are not able to remain in our own dwellings for fear of those evil-souled ones.
entries.6.27: '"'Therefore, three-eyed one, destroy them for our good. Burn the rakshasas with a mere sound of your anger, best of those who burn.'
entries.6.28: '"Hearing the gods speak thus, the slayer of Andhaka shook his head and his hand and said:
entries.6.29: '"'Those sons of Sukesha may not be slain by me in battle, gods. But I shall give you counsel by which they will be destroyed.
entries.6.30: '"'He who bears the discus and the mace in his hands, clothed in yellow, Janardana, Hari, the glorious Narayana — go to him for refuge.'
entries.6.31: '"Having received that counsel from Hara and saluted the foe of Kama, they went to Narayana's abode and laid the whole matter before him.
entries.6.32: '"Then the gods with Indra at their head were told by Narayana, 'I shall slay those enemies of the gods; be free of your fever, gods.'
entries.6.33: '"Hari has promised our destruction to the gods who fear us, bulls among rakshasas. Let us consider what may be done here.
entries.6.34: '"The death of Hiranyakashipu and of the other haters of the gods; Namuchi, Kalanemi, Samhrada best among heroes,
entries.6.35: '"Radheya of many wiles, the righteous guardian of the world, the twin Arjunas, Hardikya, Shumbha and Nishumbha —
entries.6.36: '"asuras and danavas of great courage and might, none of them is heard to have come away unconquered when he met that battle.
entries.6.37: '"All of them sacrificed with a hundred rites, all of them knew the arts of illusion, all were skilled in every weapon, all struck terror into their foes;
entries.6.38: '"and all were slain by Narayana, by hundreds and by thousands. Knowing this, you should do here what is fitting for us all."
entries.6.39: 'Then Sumali and Mali, hearing Malyavan's words, spoke to their eldest brother as Bhaga and Amsha speak to Vasava.
entries.6.40: '"We have studied, we have given and sacrificed, we have preserved our lordship; we have obtained long life free of sickness, and we have set good order upon the path.
entries.6.41: '"Plunging with our weapons into the unshakeable ocean of the gods, we have conquered foes who had no match. This fear of ours is death's own work.
entries.6.42: '"Narayana and Rudra, Shakra and Yama also — all of them fear always to stand before us.
entries.6.43: '"There is no cause at all in the god Vishnu, lord of rakshasas. It is by the fault of the gods that Vishnu's mind has been turned.
entries.6.44: '"Therefore let us make ready today, surrounded by all our forces, and seek to slay the gods themselves; from them this trouble has arisen."
entries.6.45: 'Having taken counsel thus, those mighty ones, all surrounded by their armies and proclaiming the endeavour, all those bulls among the nairritas marched out in wrath to battle, with the strength of Jambha and Vritra.
entries.6.46: 'Having so taken counsel, Rama, all those rakshasas of great bulk and great strength marched out to battle with their whole array.
entries.6.47: 'They went with chariots and elephants and horses like mountains, with asses and cattle, with camel-drawn cars, with porpoises and serpents,
entries.6.48: 'with sea-monsters, tortoises and fishes, with birds like Garuda, with lions and tigers and boars, with wild oxen and with yaks.
entries.6.49: 'Leaving Lanka, all those rakshasas went, proud of their strength; the enemies of the gods set out for the world of the gods to give battle.
entries.6.50: 'Seeing that reversal in Lanka, the beings that dwelt there grew fearful to look upon and were troubled in every way.
entries.6.51: 'Borne in their excellent chariots by hundreds and by thousands,
entries.6.52: 'the rakshasas went swiftly and with effort toward the world of the gods; and by the very road the rakshasas took, the gods withdrew.
entries.6.53: 'On earth and in the sky, dreadful portents commanded by Kala arose for the destruction of those lords of rakshasas.
entries.6.54: 'The clouds rained bones and hot blood; the oceans overpassed their shores and the mountains shook.
entries.6.55: 'Uttering loud laughter with a sound like thunder, jackals dreadful and terrible to behold howled there.
entries.6.56: 'Creatures fell and appeared one after another; and there a great wheel of vultures with fire pouring from their mouths
entries.6.57: 'circled in the sky above the rakshasas like a whirling firebrand. Red-footed pigeons and mynahs fled away; crows croaked there and cats and other beasts cried out.
entries.6.58: 'Disregarding those portents, the rakshasas, proud of their strength, went on and did not turn back, bound as they were in the noose of death.
entries.6.59: 'Malyavan and Sumali and Mali of great might went before them, as the fires go before the sacrifices.
entries.6.60: 'And all those night-rangers took refuge in Malyavan as in an unmoving mountain, as the gods take refuge in the Creator.
entries.6.61: 'That host of the lords of rakshasas, thundering like great clouds, went to the world of the gods under Mali's command, desiring victory.
entries.6.62: 'The lord Narayana, hearing from a messenger of the gods of the endeavour of the rakshasas, set his mind then upon battle.
entries.6.63: 'With his weapons and quivers made ready, seated upon the son of Vinata, having fastened on his divine armour bright as a thousand suns,
entries.6.64: 'having bound on his two spotless quivers full of arrows, and his girdle, and his spotless sword, the lotus-eyed one took up his foremost weapons — the conch, the discus, the mace, the Sharnga bow and the sword.
entries.6.65: 'Mounted then upon Suparna, the son of Vinata, huge as a mountain, the lord went with all speed for the destruction of the rakshasas.
entries.6.66: 'On Suparna's back Hari shone dark, clothed in yellow, like a rain-cloud with lightning upon the golden peak of a mountain.
entries.6.67: 'Sung by the siddhas, divine sages, great serpents, gandharvas and yakshas, bearing the discus, the sword, the Sharnga bow and the conch in his hands, he came upon those enemies who were the army of the asuras.
entries.6.68: 'That army of the rakshasa king shook, its flanks driven back by the wind of Suparna's wings, its banners whirling and its weapons scattered, as a dark mountain shakes and its rocks are loosened.
entries.6.69: 'Then the night-rangers surrounded Madhava and pierced him by thousands with their finest weapons — with arrows smeared with blood and flesh, whose forms were like the fire at the ending of an age.
entries.7.1: 'Then the rakshasas, roaring like clouds, rained a rain of arrows upon Narayana who was as a mountain, as clouds rain upon a mountain.
entries.7.2: 'Vishnu, dark and radiant, encircled by those dark chieftains of the night-rangers, was like the collyrium mountain wrapped about by raining clouds.
entries.7.3: 'As locusts fall upon a field, as gnats upon a mountain, as flies upon a jar of nectar, as sea-monsters upon the ocean,
entries.7.4: 'so the arrows loosed from the bows of the rakshasas, swift as the thunderbolt and the wind and as thought itself, entered Hari, as the worlds enter him at the dissolution.
entries.7.5: 'Those on chariots with their chariots, those on elephants' backs with their elephants, the horsemen with their horses, and the foot-soldiers standing in the sky —
entries.7.6: 'those lords of rakshasas, huge as mountains, with arrows and spears and lances and javelins left Hari no breath, as the breathing exercises leave none to a brahmin.
entries.7.7: 'Struck by the night-rangers as the great ocean is struck by its fishes, the unassailable one drew the Sharnga bow and loosed his arrows against the rakshasas.
entries.7.8: 'With sharp arrows drawn to the full and released, thunder-mouthed and swift as thought, Vishnu cut them down by hundreds and by thousands.
entries.7.9: 'Having scattered them with a rain of arrows as the wind scatters what has risen in the rains, the best of beings blew the great conch Panchajanya.
entries.7.10: 'That king of conches, born of the waters, blown by Hari with all his breath, roared with a terrible sound as though it shook the three worlds.
entries.7.11: 'The sound of that king of conches terrified the rakshasas as the lion in the forest terrifies rutting elephants.
entries.7.12: 'The horses could not keep their footing, the elephants lost their rut, and heroes fell from their chariots, weakened by the roar of the conch.
entries.7.13: 'The arrows loosed from the Sharnga bow, thunder-faced and finely feathered, tore through those rakshasas and entered the earth.
entries.7.14: 'Pierced in battle by the arrows loosed from Narayana's hand, the rakshasas fell to the ground like mountains struck by the thunderbolt.
entries.7.15: 'From the wounds made by Vishnu's discus in the enemies' limbs, blood poured in streams, as mountains pour streams of gold.
entries.7.16: 'The roar of the king of conches and the sound of the Sharnga bow, and the cries of the rakshasas too — all were swallowed by the roar of Vishnu.
entries.7.17: 'Hari cut down with his arrows their shaken necks, their shafts and banners and bows, their chariots, their flags and their quivers.
entries.7.18: 'As the fierce rays come from the sun, as the waves from the sea, as the great serpents from the mountain, as torrents of rain from a cloud,
entries.7.19: 'so the arrows loosed from the Sharnga and sped by Narayana flew swiftly forth by hundreds and by thousands.
entries.7.20: 'As lions are put to flight by the sharabha, as elephants by the lion, as tigers by the elephant, as leopards by the tiger,
entries.7.21: 'as dogs by the leopard, as cats by the dog, as snakes by the cat, and as mice by the snake,
entries.7.22: 'so all those rakshasas were driven before Vishnu the mighty; some fled, others were put to flight, and others were laid low upon the earth.
entries.7.23: 'Having slain the rakshasas by thousands, the slayer of Madhu filled his conch as the king of the gods fills a cloud.
entries.7.24: 'Terrified by Narayana's arrows and overwhelmed by the blast of the conch, the broken army of the rakshasas turned toward Lanka.
entries.7.25: 'When the army of the rakshasas was broken and struck down by Narayana's arrows, Sumali held Hari back in the battle with a rain of arrows.
entries.7.26: 'He covered him as mist covers the sun, and the rakshasas, being brave, took heart again.
entries.7.27: 'Then that rakshasa, proud of his strength, rushed forward in fury, uttering a great roar as though giving life back to the rakshasas.
entries.7.28: 'Tossing his long ornaments and shaking his arm as an elephant shakes its trunk, the rakshasa roared for joy like a thundercloud lit with lightning.
entries.7.29: 'As Sumali roared, Hari cut off the head of his charioteer with its blazing earrings, and the rakshasa's horses ran wild.
entries.7.30: 'Carried away by those maddened horses, Sumali, lord of rakshasas, was whirled about as a man without resolve is whirled by the runaway horses of his senses.
entries.7.31: 'Then, when Sumali's horses had carried off his chariot, Malyavan turned toward Vishnu's chariot as the mighty-armed one bore down upon the field.
entries.7.32: 'And Mali too came on, taking up his bow with its arrows. The arrows loosed from Mali's bow, adorned with gold, reached Hari and entered him as birds enter the Krauncha mountain.
entries.7.33: 'Though tormented by the thousands of arrows loosed by Mali, Vishnu was not shaken in that battle, as one who has conquered his senses is not shaken by afflictions.
entries.7.34: 'Then the lord, the maker of beings and destroyer of foes, sounded his bowstring and loosed floods of arrows at Mali.
entries.7.35: 'Those arrows, bright as the thunderbolt and the lightning, reached Mali's body and drank his blood as serpents drink nectar.
entries.7.36: 'The bearer of the conch, the discus and the mace turned Mali back, and struck down his crown, his banner, his bow and his horses.
entries.7.37: 'Deprived of his chariot, Mali, best of the night-rangers, took up his mace and sprang forward with it in his hand like a lion from a mountain peak.
entries.7.38: 'With that mace he struck the lord of Garuda upon the forehead, as Antaka strikes Ishana, as Indra strikes a mountain with his thunderbolt.
entries.7.39: 'Struck hard by Mali with that mace, Garuda was overcome with pain and carried the god away from the battle with his face turned aside.
entries.7.40: 'When the god had been so turned aside by Mali through Garuda, a great cry arose from the rakshasas roaring in triumph.
entries.7.41: 'Hearing the shouting of the rakshasas as they roared, the younger brother of Indra —
entries.7.42: 'the lord Hari, greatly angered, held himself sideways upon the king of birds and, though turned away, loosed his discus at Mali to slay him.
entries.7.43: 'That discus, bright as the disc of the sun, lighting the sky with its own radiance, like the wheel of time itself, struck down Mali's head.
entries.7.44: 'The dreadful head of that lord of rakshasas, severed by the discus, fell pouring blood as Rahu's head fell of old.
entries.7.45: 'Then from the gods, all rejoicing and crying out with all their breath, there rose the roar of a lion's shout and the cry "Well done, god!"
entries.7.46: 'Seeing Mali slain, Sumali and Malyavan too, with their forces, burning with grief, fled straight toward Lanka.
entries.7.47: 'And Garuda, recovered, turned back as before and, roused to anger, scattered the rakshasas with the wind of his wings.
entries.7.48: 'Their lotus-faces cut off by the discus, their chests crushed by the mace, their necks broken by the plough-weapon, their heads split by the pestle,
entries.7.49: 'some cut down by the sword and others tormented by arrows, the rakshasas fell swiftly from the sky into the waters of the ocean.
entries.7.50: 'Narayana tore apart with the thunderbolts of his finest arrows, loosed from his bow, the night-rangers with their hair loosened and flying, as great clouds with lightning tear the sky with their bolts.
entries.7.51: 'Its parasols broken, its weapons falling, its trim array shattered by arrows, its entrails spilled out, its eyes rolling with fear, that army became like a thing gone mad.
entries.7.52: 'The cries and the rushing of those night-rangers, together with their elephants, were like the cries and rushing of elephants tormented by a lion, as they were crushed by that ancient lion.
entries.7.53: 'Held back by the nets of Hari's arrows, loosing their own nets of arrows in return, those night-rangers ran like dark clouds of doom scattered by the wind.
entries.7.54: 'Their heads cut off by strokes of the discus, their limbs crushed by blows of the mace, split apart in two ways by his onslaught, those lords of rakshasas fell like mountains.
entries.7.55: 'With their jewelled necklaces and earrings swaying, those night-rangers like dark rain-clouds, as they were struck down without pause, seemed like dark mountains being cast down.
entries.8.1: 'When that army was being destroyed from behind by the lotus-navelled one, Malyavan turned back, as the ocean turns when it comes to its shore.
entries.8.2: 'His eyes red with anger and his crown shaking, that night-ranger spoke these words to the lotus-navelled one, best of beings.
entries.8.3: '"Narayana, you do not know the ancient law of the kshatriya. You slay us who are afraid and whose minds are not upon the fight, as any common man might.
entries.8.4: '"Whoever, be he asura or other, commits the sin of slaying one whose face is turned away — that slayer does not go to the heaven that the doers of merit attain.
entries.8.5: '"But if you have any appetite for battle, bearer of the conch, the discus and the mace, here I stand. Show me what strength is yours, and let me see it."
entries.8.6: 'Seeing Malyavan standing there like the Malyavan mountain, the mighty younger brother of the king of the gods said to that lord of rakshasas:
entries.8.7: '"I gave the gods safety when they were afraid of you, and I promised the destruction of the rakshasas. That promise is now being kept.
entries.8.8: '"What pleases the gods must always be done by me, even at the cost of my life. Therefore I shall destroy you, even if you go down to the nether world."
entries.8.9: 'As the god of gods with eyes like red lotuses was speaking, the lord of rakshasas in great anger pierced him between the shoulders with a spear.
entries.8.10: 'That spear, loosed from Malyavan's arm and sounding like a bell, blazed upon Hari's breast like lightning in a cloud.
entries.8.11: 'Then the lotus-eyed one, dear to the bearer of the spear, drew out that very spear and hurled it back at Malyavan.
entries.8.12: 'That spear, loosed from Govinda's hand as though by Skanda, sought out the rakshasa and flew like Mahendra's bolt at the collyrium mountain.
entries.8.13: 'It fell upon the broad chest of that lord of rakshasas, bright with the weight of his necklaces, as the thunderbolt falls upon a mountain peak.
entries.8.14: 'His armour split by it, he entered a great darkness; but Malyavan revived and stood again like an unmoving mountain.
entries.8.15: 'Then he took up an iron pike thick with spikes and struck the god firmly between the breasts.
entries.8.16: 'Then, still hungry for the fight, the night-ranger struck the younger brother of Vasava with his fist and withdrew a bow's length.
entries.8.17: 'Then a great cry of "Well done, well done!" arose in the sky; and having struck Vishnu, the rakshasa struck Garuda also.
entries.8.18: 'Then the son of Vinata in his anger drove the rakshasa off with the wind of his wings, as a strong wind drives a heap of dry leaves.
entries.8.19: 'Seeing his elder brother driven back by the wind of the king of birds' wings, Sumali with his forces turned toward Lanka.
entries.8.20: 'And the rakshasa Malyavan too, tossed by the force of that wind, rejoined his own army and went to Lanka, covered with shame.
entries.8.21: 'Thus, lotus-eyed one, were those rakshasas broken again and again in battle by Hari, and their foremost leaders slain.
entries.8.22: 'Being unable to fight against Vishnu, and tormented by fear, they left Lanka and went with their wives to dwell in the nether world.
entries.8.23: 'Coming to the rakshasa Sumali, best of the Raghus, those of renowned valour lived on in the line of Salakatankata.
entries.8.24: 'But those whom you have slain are the rakshasas called the sons of Pulastya. Sumali, Malyavan, Mali, and those who went before them —
entries.8.25: 'all those greatly blessed ones were mightier than Ravana.
entries.8.26: 'And there is no other slayer of the rakshasas, those enemies of the gods and thorns in their side, but the god Narayana, bearer of the conch, the discus and the mace.
entries.8.27: 'You are that god Narayana, four-armed and eternal, born to slay the rakshasas — unconquerable, lord and imperishable.
entries.8.28: 'You are the restorer of dharma when its order is lost, the maker of creatures age after age; you are born for the destruction of the wicked, and you love those who come to you for refuge.
entries.8.29: 'Thus, king of men, I have told you today the whole origin of the rakshasas as it truly was. Hear further, best of the Raghus, all the unequalled power of Ravana's birth and of his sons.
entries.8.30: 'For a long time that rakshasa Sumali, tormented by fear of Vishnu, wandered in the nether world; and afterwards the mighty one, together with his sons and grandsons — while the lord of wealth dwelt in Lanka.'
entries.9.1: 'After some time the rakshasa named Sumali came up from the nether world and wandered over all the world of mortals.
entries.9.2: 'He was like a dark rain-cloud, with earrings of burnished gold, and he took with him his maiden daughter, who was like Shri without her lotus.
entries.9.3: 'As that lord of rakshasas wandered over the face of the earth, he saw the lord of wealth going by in the Pushpaka —
entries.9.4: 'the mighty son of Pulastya, going to see his father. Seeing him, like an immortal, moving at his will and resembling the sun,
entries.9.5: 'he who had entered the nether world from the world of men was filled with wonder; and that great-minded one among rakshasas thought thus:
entries.9.6: '"What is best to be done, and how may we prosper?" Then the rakshasa said to his daughter, Kaikasi by name:
entries.9.7: '"Daughter, this is the time for your giving in marriage, and your youth is passing. Out of fear of refusal you are not sought by suitors,
entries.9.8: '"and for your sake we are all held bound, though our minds are set on dharma. You are endowed with every virtue, little daughter, like Shri herself made visible. To be the father of a daughter is a sorrow to all who care for their honour,
entries.9.9: '"and it is not known who may seek the maiden's hand, my child.
entries.9.10: '"You are endowed with every virtue, little daughter, like Shri herself made visible. The mother's family, the father's family, and the family into which she is given — a maiden keeps all three lines always in suspense.
entries.9.11: '"Go then, daughter, to the best of great sages, born of Prajapati's line; go to Vishrava, the son of Pulastya, and choose him yourself.
entries.9.12: '"Such sons will be born to you, daughter, and of that there is no doubt — sons equal in splendour to the sun, such as this lord of wealth."
entries.9.13: 'Hearing those words of her father, the maiden out of respect for him went and stood where Vishrava was performing his penance.
entries.9.14: 'At that very moment, Rama, the twice-born son of Pulastya was tending the sacred fire, himself like a fourth flame beside it.
entries.9.15: 'Without regard for that dreadful hour, out of respect for her father, she approached and stood before him with her face bent toward his feet, that lovely one scratching the ground again and again with the tip of her toe.
entries.9.16: 'Seeing her fair form and her face like the full moon, radiant with her own light, that most generous one said:
entries.9.17: '"Good lady, whose daughter are you, and from where have you come here? What is your business, and for what reason? Tell me truly, fair one."
entries.9.18: 'Being addressed thus, the maiden joined her palms and said, "By your own power, sage, you are able to know my mind.
entries.9.19: '"Yet know me, brahmarshi, to have come at my father's command. My name is Kaikasi, and the rest you are able to know."
entries.9.20: 'The sage entered into meditation and then said these words: "I have understood, good lady, the reason that is in your mind.
entries.9.21: '"You desire sons by me, you who move like a rutting elephant. But because you have come to me at this dreadful hour,
entries.9.22: '"hear then, good lady, what manner of sons you will bear — dreadful, dreadful of form, and delighting in dreadful company.
entries.9.23: '"You will bring forth rakshasas of cruel deeds, fair one." Hearing those words, she bowed low and said:
entries.9.24: '"Venerable one, I do not wish for such sons from you, a speaker of the Veda — sons of so evil a conduct. Be gracious to me."
entries.9.25: 'Being addressed thus by the maiden, Vishrava, that bull among sages, spoke again to Kaikasi as the full moon speaks to Rohini:
entries.9.26: '"The last son who will be born to you, fair-faced one, will be worthy of my line and devoted to dharma."
entries.9.27: 'Being told this, Rama, that maiden after some time brought forth a hideous shape, a rakshasa most dreadful —
entries.9.28: 'ten-necked, with great tusks, like a heap of dark collyrium, with copper-coloured lips, twenty arms, a huge mouth and blazing hair.
entries.9.29: 'At the moment of his birth jackals with flaming mouths and the eaters of raw flesh circled from right to left.
entries.9.30: 'The god rained blood, the clouds cried harshly, the sun did not shine, and great meteors fell upon the earth.
entries.9.31: 'The earth shook and dreadful winds blew, and the ocean, lord of rivers, unshakeable though it is, was troubled.
entries.9.32: 'Then his father, the equal of the Grandsire, gave him a name: "This one is born with ten necks; he shall be Dashagriva."
entries.9.33: 'After him was born the mighty Kumbhakarna, whose bulk had no measure to match it in this world.
entries.9.34: 'Then was born Shurpanakha of the misshapen face; and Vibhishana, devoted to dharma, was Kaikasi's last son.
entries.9.35: 'At the birth of that one of great courage a rain of flowers fell.
entries.9.36: 'The drums of the gods sounded in the sky, and a voice in the air spoke then, saying, "Well done, well done."
entries.9.37: 'Those two of great might, Kumbhakarna and Dashagriva, grew up there in the great forest, striking terror into the world.
entries.9.38: 'Kumbhakarna in his wildness devoured great sages devoted to dharma and ranged about, never satisfied, eating up the three worlds.
entries.9.39: 'But Vibhishana, devoted to dharma, was ever established in dharma; he lived with his senses conquered, given to the study of the sacred texts and restrained in his food.
entries.9.40: 'Then after some time the god Vaishravana, lord of wealth, came there in the Pushpaka to see his father.
entries.9.41: 'Seeing him blazing there with splendour, the rakshasi Kaikasi came and said to Dashagriva:
entries.9.42: '"Son, look at your brother Vaishravana, clothed in splendour. Though you are brothers alike, look at yourself, in such a state as this.
entries.9.43: '"Dashagriva of measureless valour, make such effort, my son, that you may become the equal of Vaishravana."
entries.9.44: 'Hearing his mother's words, the mighty Dashagriva conceived a matchless indignation and made a vow.
entries.9.45: '"I promise you truly: I shall become my brother's equal or more than his equal in strength. Put away the grief that is in your heart."
entries.9.46: 'Then in that same anger Dashagriva with his younger brothers, desiring to perform a hard task, set his mind upon penance.
entries.9.47: 'Resolving, "By penance I shall obtain my desire," he came for the accomplishment of his purpose to the holy hermitage of Gokarna.
entries.9.48: 'There that rakshasa of fierce valour, with his younger brothers, performed a matchless penance and satisfied the mighty Grandsire; and being pleased, he gave them boons that brought victory.'
entries.10.1: Then Rama said to the sage, 'How was it with those brothers in the forest? What manner of penance did those mighty ones perform there, brahmin?'
entries.10.2: Agastya said to Rama, whose heart was well pleased: 'Those brothers took up there, each of them, the several observances of dharma.
entries.10.3: 'Kumbhakarna, ever intent and standing on the path of dharma, endured in the hot season, surrounded by the five fires.
entries.10.4: 'In the rains he was drenched by the water of the clouds and kept the hero's posture; and always in the cold season he made his dwelling in the midst of water.
entries.10.5: 'Thus ten thousand years passed for him as he strove in dharma and stood firm upon the good path.
entries.10.6: 'And Vibhishana, devoted to dharma, ever intent upon dharma and pure, stood upon one foot for five thousand years.
entries.10.7: 'When his observance was complete the hosts of apsaras danced, a rain of flowers fell, and the gods were stirred.
entries.10.8: 'For five thousand years he faced the sun, standing with his head and arms upraised, his mind fixed upon the study of the sacred texts.
entries.10.9: 'Thus ten thousand years passed for Vibhishana of the disciplined soul, as though he were in heaven in the Nandana grove.
entries.10.10: 'And Dashagriva went without food for ten thousand years; and at the end of each thousand years he offered a head into the fire.
entries.10.11: 'Thus nine thousand years passed for him, and nine of his heads entered the fire.
entries.10.12: 'Then in the ten-thousandth year, when Dashagriva was minded to cut off his tenth head, the Grandsire came there.
entries.10.13: 'The Grandsire, well pleased, came attended by the gods and said, "Dashagriva, I am pleased with you.
entries.10.14: '"Choose quickly, knower of dharma, whatever boon you desire. What wish of yours shall I fulfil today? Your labour shall not be in vain."
entries.10.15: 'Then Dashagriva, with a heart full of joy, bowed his head to the god and spoke in a voice faltering with gladness:
entries.10.16: '"Lord, for living creatures there is no fear from anything but death. There is no enemy like death; I choose deathlessness."
entries.10.17: 'Being addressed thus, Brahma said to Dashagriva: "Complete deathlessness is not for you. Choose some other boon from me."
entries.10.18: 'Being told this, Rama, by Brahma the maker of the worlds, Dashagriva said this before him with joined palms:
entries.10.19: '"Let me be one who cannot be slain by suparnas, nagas or yakshas, by daityas, danavas or rakshasas, nor by the gods, overseer of creatures, eternal one.
entries.10.20: '"I have no concern about other living creatures, honoured of the immortals. Men and the rest I count as no more than blades of grass."
entries.10.21: 'Being addressed thus by the rakshasa Dashagriva, that soul of dharma, the god and Grandsire, spoke with the gods beside him:
entries.10.22: '"This word of yours shall be so, bull among rakshasas." Having said this to Dashagriva, Rama, the Grandsire went on:
entries.10.23: '"Hear a further boon from me, an auspicious one, for I am pleased. Those heads which you offered before into the fire, sinless one,
entries.10.24: '"they shall be yours again as they were, rakshasa. And I grant you here, gentle one, another boon hard for any to obtain:
entries.10.25: '"your form shall be at your will, whatever your mind desires — there is no doubt of it, rakshasa, by this boon of mine."
entries.10.26: 'When the Grandsire had spoken thus to the rakshasa Dashagriva, the heads he had offered into the fire rose up again.
entries.10.27: 'Having said this to Dashagriva, Rama, the Grandsire of the worlds then spoke to Vibhishana:
entries.10.28: '"Vibhishana, my child, I am well pleased with you, whose mind is joined to dharma. Choose a boon, soul of dharma, faithful to your vows."
entries.10.29: 'And Vibhishana, devoted to dharma, ever encircled by all virtues as the moon by its rays, spoke with joined palms:
entries.10.30: '"Lord, I am fulfilled, in that the teacher of the worlds himself has come to me. If a boon is to be given by one who is pleased, hear mine, holder of good vows.
entries.10.31: '"Let my mind be upon dharma even in the greatest calamity; and let the brahmastra, though untaught, shine forth in me, lord.
entries.10.32: '"Whatever thought arises in me, in whatever stage of life I may be, let it be righteous, and let me keep that dharma.
entries.10.33: '"This, most generous one, is the highest boon I can conceive. For those who love dharma there is nothing hard to obtain in this world."
entries.10.34: 'Prajapati, pleased again, said to Vibhishana: "Since you are so devoted to dharma, my child, so shall it be.
entries.10.35: '"Since, though born in the womb of the rakshasas, destroyer of foes, your mind does not turn to unrighteousness, I grant you deathlessness."
entries.10.36: 'Having said this, when Prajapati stood ready to grant a boon to Kumbhakarna, all the gods spoke to him with joined palms:
entries.10.37: '"You should not grant a boon to Kumbhakarna. You know how this evil-minded one terrifies the worlds.
entries.10.38: '"In the Nandana grove he has devoured seven apsaras and ten of Mahendra's followers, brahmin, and sages and men besides.
entries.10.39: '"If the rakshasa did such things before he had any boon, then having won one he would devour the three worlds.
entries.10.40: '"Under the pretext of a boon let stupor be given to him, one of measureless splendour. So it will be well for the worlds, and he will be humbled."
entries.10.41: 'Being addressed thus by the gods, Brahma the lotus-born considered; and as he considered, the goddess Sarasvati came to his side.
entries.10.42: 'Standing beside him with joined palms, Sarasvati said, "Here I am, god. What task shall I perform?"
entries.10.43: 'Prajapati said to Sarasvati who had come, "Vani, be to this lord of rakshasas what the gods desire."
entries.10.44: 'Saying "So be it," she entered into him; and Prajapati said, "Mighty-armed Kumbhakarna, choose the boon you have in mind."
entries.10.45: 'Kumbhakarna, hearing those words, said, "God of gods, my desire is to sleep for many years."
entries.10.46: 'Saying "So be it" to him, Brahma departed with the gods; and the goddess Sarasvati left the rakshasa again.
entries.10.47: 'When Brahma with the gods had gone up into the sky, he was released by Sarasvati and came back to his own senses.
entries.10.48: 'Then Kumbhakarna, evil-souled, thought in his sorrow, "What is this word that has fallen from my mouth today?
entries.10.49: '"I think I have been deluded by the gods who came here." Thus all those brothers of blazing splendour obtained their boons; and going to the Shleshmataka wood, they dwelt there in ease.'
entries.11.1: 'When Sumali learned that those night-rangers had received their boons, he cast off fear and rose up from the nether world with his followers.
entries.11.2: 'Maricha and Prahasta, Virupaksha and Mahodara, the ministers of that rakshasa, rose up with him in great eagerness.
entries.11.3: 'Sumali, surrounded by his ministers and by the bulls among rakshasas, came to Dashagriva, embraced him and said:
entries.11.4: '"By good fortune, child, this longed-for wish of yours has been fulfilled, in that you have won the highest boon from the best of the three worlds.
entries.11.5: '"That great fear of Vishnu, for whose sake we left Lanka and went to the nether world, is now gone from us, mighty-armed one.
entries.11.6: '"More than once, terrified by that fear, we abandoned our own dwelling and fled together and entered the nether world.
entries.11.7: '"And this city Lanka is ours, fitted for rakshasas; it has been settled by your brother, the wise lord of wealth.
entries.11.8: '"If it can be had here by conciliation or by gift, sinless one, or by force, mighty-armed one, then let it be recovered and the thing is done.
entries.11.9: '"You shall be lord of Lanka, dear child, and of that there is no doubt. By you this line of rakshasas, though sunk, has been raised again; and you shall be lord over us all, mighty one."
entries.11.10: 'Then Dashagriva said to his grandfather who stood before him, "The lord of wealth is our elder; you should not speak in such a way."
entries.11.11: 'Being refused even by conciliation by that great lord of rakshasas, the rakshasa said nothing then, knowing what he intended.
entries.11.12: 'After some time, when Ravana was at his ease, the night-ranger spoke to Dashagriva, who had spoken so —
entries.11.13: 'Prahasta spoke this respectful word, and gave his reason.
entries.11.14: '"Dashagriva, mighty-armed one, you should not speak in such a way. Among heroes there is no brotherhood; hear this word of mine.
entries.11.15: '"Aditi and Diti were sisters together, both wives of surpassing beauty of Kashyapa, the lord of creatures.
entries.11.16: '"Aditi bore the gods, the lords of the three worlds; and Diti bore sons who sprang from Kashyapa himself.
entries.11.17: '"This city, knower of dharma, and the earth with its forests and oceans and its mountains, belonged of old to the daityas, and they were the masters of it.
entries.11.18: '"But Vishnu the mighty slew them in battle, and this imperishable threefold world was brought under the sway of the gods.
entries.11.19: '"You alone would not be doing something unheard of by this reversal; it has been the practice of gods and asuras alike. Do therefore as I say."
entries.11.20: 'Being addressed thus, Dashagriva, with a heart full of gladness, considered for a moment and then said, "So be it."
entries.11.21: 'And on that very day, in that same joy, the valiant Dashagriva went to the forest with those night-rangers.
entries.11.22: 'Then, staying upon Trikuta, that night-ranger Dashagriva sent Prahasta, who was skilled in speech, as his envoy.
entries.11.23: '"Go quickly, Prahasta, and say to that bull among the nairritas, to the lord of wealth, this word from me, and put conciliation first.
entries.11.24: '"'This city Lanka, king, belongs to the great-souled rakshasas. It was settled by you, gentle one, but this is not fitting for you, sinless one.
entries.11.25: '"'If therefore you would give it to us today, one of unmatched valour, my joy would be made and dharma would be preserved.'"
entries.11.26: 'And he went to the city of Lanka, well guarded by the giver of wealth, and spoke these most courteous words to the keeper of riches:
entries.11.27: '"I have been sent to you by your brother Dashagriva, holder of good vows, mighty-armed one, best of all who bear arms.
entries.11.28: '"Let it be heard, one of great wisdom, skilled in all the sciences — hear from me, lord of wealth, what Dashanana says.
entries.11.29: '"'This lovely city, wide-eyed one, was enjoyed of old by the rakshasas of terrible valour, with Sumali at their head.
entries.11.30: '"'This is now made known to you, son of Vishrava. Let it therefore be given, dear one, since he asks it of you in a spirit of conciliation.'"
entries.11.31: 'Hearing that word from Prahasta, the god Vaishravana, skilled in speech, answered him:
entries.11.32: '"This Lanka was given to me by my father when it was empty of night-rangers; and I have settled it with yakshas by my gifts and honours and other virtues.
entries.11.33: '"Go and tell Dashagriva: what city and what kingdom are mine are yours also, mighty-armed one. Enjoy the kingdom without a thorn in it."
entries.11.34: 'Having spoken thus, the lord of wealth went into his father's presence.
entries.11.35: 'Saluting his elder, he told him what Ravana desired: "Father, this Dashagriva has sent an envoy to me,
entries.11.36: '"saying, 'Let the city of Lanka be given, which was dwelt in before by the hosts of rakshasas.' Tell me, holder of good vows, what I should do in this."
entries.11.37: 'Being addressed thus, the brahmarshi Vishrava, that bull among sages, said to the giver of wealth who stood with joined palms, "Hear my word, my son.
entries.11.38: '"The mighty-armed Dashagriva spoke to me in my presence, and I rebuked him and said much to that evil-minded one.
entries.11.39: '"I spoke to him in anger, and he goes to ruin again and again. Hear my word, my son, which is for your good and joined with dharma.
entries.11.40: '"That evil-minded one, bewildered by the granting of his boon, does not know the honoured from the unhonoured; and by my curse he has come to a dreadful nature.
entries.11.41: '"Therefore go, mighty-armed one, to Kailasa which upholds the earth, and make your dwelling there; leave Lanka and go with your followers.
entries.11.42: '"There the lovely Mandakini flows, best of rivers, her waters covered with golden lotuses bright as the sun,
entries.11.43: '"and with white lilies and blue lotuses and other fragrant flowers besides.
entries.11.44: '"There the gods with the gandharvas, the apsaras, the serpents and the kinnaras, given to sport, take their pleasure always and dwell there ever.
entries.11.45: '"It is not fitting that you should have enmity with this rakshasa, giver of wealth. You know what a supreme boon he has obtained."
entries.11.46: 'Being told this, out of respect for his father he took that word at once, and went with his wives and children, his followers, his mounts and his wealth.
entries.11.47: 'Then Prahasta went to Dashagriva and, with a glad heart, spoke to that great one who sat with his ministers and his younger brothers:
entries.11.48: '"The city of Lanka stands empty; the giver of wealth has left it and gone. Enter it with us and maintain your own dharma."
entries.11.49: 'Being addressed thus by Prahasta, the mighty Dashagriva entered the city of Lanka with his brothers and his forces and followers.
entries.11.50: 'That enemy of the gods ascended into the city abandoned by the giver of wealth, with its great highways well laid out, as the lord of the gods ascends to heaven.
entries.11.51: 'And being consecrated then by the night-rangers, Dashanana settled the city; and that city became full to overflowing with night-rangers like dark rain-clouds.
entries.11.52: 'The lord of wealth, out of respect for his father's word, settled his city upon the mountain white as the moon, adorned with excellent and well-decked dwellings, as Purandara settled Amaravati.'
entries.12.1: 'When the lord of rakshasas had been consecrated together with his two brothers, he then gave thought to the giving of his rakshasi sister in marriage.
entries.12.2: 'He gave his rakshasi sister, Shurpanakha by name, to the lord of danavas of the Kalakeya line, whose name was Vidyujjihva.
entries.12.3: 'Then, having given her, the rakshasa went out hunting on his own; and there, Rama, he saw Maya, the son of Diti.
entries.12.4: 'Seeing him with a maiden beside him, the night-ranger Dashagriva asked, "Who are you, alone in a forest empty of men and beasts? And why do you stay here with this doe-eyed one?"
entries.12.5: 'Maya, Rama, answered the night-ranger who asked him: "Let it be heard; I shall tell you all that has befallen me.
entries.12.6: '"There was an apsara named Hema, dear one, if you have heard of her before. She was given to me by the gods as Paulomi was given to Shatakratu.
entries.12.7: '"For five hundred years my mind was bound to her, dear one. Then she went upon the business of the gods, and thirteen years passed.
entries.12.8: '"And in the fourteenth year I built by my magic a city all of gold, wonderful with diamond and beryl.
entries.12.9: '"There I dwelt wretched, bereft of her and greatly grieving.
entries.12.10: '"From that city I took my daughter and came to the forest. This is my daughter, king, born of her womb and reared there.
entries.12.11: '"I have come with her to seek a husband for her. To be the father of a daughter is a sorrow to all who care for their honour,
entries.12.12: '"for a daughter keeps two families always in suspense. And two sons also were born to me of that wife.
entries.12.13: '"Mayavi was the first, dear one, and Dundubhi after him. Thus I have told you everything truly, since you asked.
entries.12.14: '"But now, dear one, how shall I know who you are?" Being addressed thus, the rakshasa answered him modestly:
entries.12.15: '"I am the son of Pulastya's line, Dashagriva by name — of the sage Vishrava, who was the third from Brahma."
entries.12.16: 'Being told this, Rama, by the lord of rakshasas, the danava Maya, knowing him to be the son of a great sage, was filled with joy, and was pleased to give his daughter to him there and then.
entries.12.17: 'Then Maya took her hand and placed it in his, and the lord of daityas said smiling to the lord of rakshasas:
entries.12.18: '"This is my daughter, king, borne by the apsara Hema — the maiden Mandodari. Take her as your wife."
entries.12.19: 'Dashagriva said to him, "So be it," Rama; and there he kindled the fire and took her hand in marriage.
entries.12.20: 'For Maya, Rama, knew of the curse laid upon him by the ascetic; and knowing it, he gave her to him because his line came from the Grandsire.
entries.12.21: 'And he gave him also that unfailing spear of surpassing wonder, won by great austerity — the spear with which he struck down Lakshmana.
entries.12.22: 'Having thus taken a wife, the lord and master of Lanka went to the city and brought wives for his two brothers.
entries.12.23: 'Ravana appointed as Kumbhakarna's wife the granddaughter of Vairochana, Vajrajvala by name.
entries.12.24: 'And Vibhishana took as wife the daughter of Shailusha, the great-souled king of the gandharvas — Sarama, a knower of dharma.
entries.12.25: 'She was born on the shore of Lake Manasa; and at that time the lake Manasa swelled with the coming of the rains.
entries.12.26: 'And the mother of that maiden cried out in her love, "Lake, do not swell" — sara ma — and from that she became Sarama.
entries.12.27: 'Thus those rakshasas took their wives and made merry there, each coming to his own wife, like gandharvas in the Nandana grove.
entries.12.28: 'Then Mandodari bore a son, Meghanada — he whom you call Indrajit.
entries.12.29: 'At the very moment of his birth that son of Ravana, as he cried, uttered a great roar like a thundercloud.
entries.12.30: 'And Lanka was stunned by that roar, Raghava; so his father himself gave him the name Meghanada.
entries.12.31: 'And he grew, Rama, in Ravana's fair inner apartments, guarded by the best of women, hidden like fire within kindling,
entries.12.32: 'that son of Ravana, bringing great joy to his mother and his father.'
entries.13.1: 'Then after some time the sleep sent by the lord of the worlds came upon Kumbhakarna, taking form and heavy upon him.
entries.13.2: 'Then Kumbhakarna said to his brother, who was seated there, "Sleep oppresses me, king. Have a dwelling made for me."
entries.13.3: 'Then craftsmen were appointed by the king, skilled as Vishvakarma, and they made for Kumbhakarna a bright hall a yojana broad and twice as long,
entries.13.4: 'lovely to behold and free of all disturbance, adorned everywhere with pillars of crystal and of wrought gold,
entries.13.5: 'with steps of beryl and a network of little bells, set with archways of ivory and terraces of diamond and crystal.
entries.13.6: 'The rakshasa had it made delightful and full of every comfort, giving ease always in every part, like a holy cave of Meru.
entries.13.7: 'There the mighty Kumbhakarna, overcome by sleep, lay for many thousands of years and did not wake.
entries.13.8: 'And while Kumbhakarna was overcome by sleep, Dashanana, with none to check him, slew gods and sages, yakshas and gandharvas.
entries.13.9: 'He went to the beautiful gardens, the Nandana and the rest, and in great fury Dashanana broke them down.
entries.13.10: 'Sporting as an elephant sports in a river, tossing trees as the wind tosses them, that rakshasa laid waste the groves like a loosed thunderbolt.
entries.13.11: 'Learning that Dashagriva behaved so, the lord of wealth, who knew dharma, and remembering the conduct that befitted his own family,
entries.13.12: 'sent an envoy then to Lanka in the spirit of brotherhood, for Dashagriva's own good.
entries.13.13: 'He went to the city of Lanka and came to Vibhishana, who honoured him according to dharma and asked the reason of his coming.
entries.13.14: 'And Vibhishana, having asked after the welfare of the king and of their kinsmen, brought him before Dashanana, who was seated in the assembly hall.
entries.13.15: 'Seeing the king there, blazing with his own splendour, he honoured him with the word "Victory!" and then stood silent.
entries.13.16: 'To Dashagriva, seated there upon a fine couch bright with excellent coverings, the envoy then spoke:
entries.13.17: '"King, I shall tell you all that your brother has said — words worthy both of your conduct and of your family, hero.
entries.13.18: '"'Enough now, it is sufficient; you have gathered a name for your deeds. It is well that you should stand firm in dharma, if it can be done.
entries.13.19: '"'I have seen the Nandana grove broken, I have heard that sages are slain, and I have heard, king, of the gods' preparations against you.
entries.13.20: '"'And I have been slighted by you many times, lord of rakshasas. Yet one's own kinsmen are dear, and offend out of childishness.
entries.13.21: '"'For my part I went to the slopes of Himavat to serve dharma, taking up a fierce observance, restrained and with my senses controlled.
entries.13.22: '"'There I saw the god and his consort, the lord and his lady; and by chance my left eye fell upon the goddess there.
entries.13.23: '"'"Who may this fair one be?" I thought — for no other reason at all; for Rudrani stood there having taken on a beauty beyond compare.
entries.13.24: '"'By the divine power of the goddess my left eye was burnt, and its light, like a lamp choked with dust, turned tawny.
entries.13.25: '"'Then I went to another broad slope of that mountain and held in silence a great vow for eight hundred years.
entries.13.26: '"'When that observance was complete, the god Maheshvara, being pleased, spoke these words there with a pleased heart:
entries.13.27: '"'"The tawniness that came upon you from looking on the goddess's form — I am pleased with you, knower of dharma, for this penance, holder of good vows.
entries.13.28: '"'"This vow has been kept by me and by you alone, lord of wealth. There is no third man who would keep such a vow.
entries.13.29: '"'"This is a vow of firm resolve, brought forth by me long ago. Take pleasure then, gentle one, in friendship with me, lord of wealth.
entries.13.30: '"'"You have won me by your penance; be my friend, sinless one. And as for your left eye, burnt by the goddess's power,
entries.13.31: '"'"the name One-tawny-eyed shall remain yours for ever."' Having thus gained friendship with him and taken leave of Shankara,
entries.13.32: '"'and having come away, I heard of this evil resolve of yours.
entries.13.33: '"'Turn back therefore from this consorting with unrighteousness, which is the ruin of your family. For the gods with the hosts of sages are considering the means of your death.'"
entries.13.34: 'Being addressed thus, Dashagriva, his eyes red with anger, ground his hands and his teeth together and spoke these words:
entries.13.35: '"I have understood, envoy, the words you speak. But this is not yours, nor is it his, by whom as a brother you were sent.
entries.13.36: '"This keeper of riches does not speak here for my good. As for his friendship with Maheshvara — the fool would have me hear of it!
entries.13.37: '"Nor can I pardon what you have said. What I have borne with all this while, envoy, I have borne for his sake.
entries.13.38: '"'He must not be killed by me, for he is my elder and my superior' — so I have thought. But now, having heard his words, this is my resolve:
entries.13.39: '"leaning upon the strength of my arms, I shall conquer the three worlds as well.
entries.13.40: '"This very hour, and for that one man's sake, I shall send those four guardians of the world to the house of Yama."
entries.13.41: 'Having spoken thus, the lord of Lanka struck the envoy down with his sword and gave him to the evil-souled rakshasas to devour.
entries.13.42: 'Then, having performed the rites for a safe journey, Ravana mounted his chariot and went, longing to conquer the three worlds, to where the lord of wealth was.'
entries.14.1: 'Then, with his six ministers who were ever swollen with strength — Mahodara and Prahasta, Maricha, Shuka and Sarana,
entries.14.2: 'and the hero Dhumraksha, ever greedy for battle — surrounded by these, the glorious one set out, as though burning up the worlds in his anger.
entries.14.3: 'Passing over cities and rivers and mountains, forests and groves, in a moment he reached the mountain Kailasa.
entries.14.4: 'Learning that the lord of rakshasas had settled upon that mountain — that evil-souled one with his counsellors, exceedingly eager for battle —
entries.14.5: 'the yakshas could not stand before that rakshasa. Knowing him to be the king's brother, they went to where the lord of wealth was.
entries.14.6: 'They went and told him all that his brother intended; and being given leave by the giver of wealth, they went gladly to the fight.
entries.14.7: 'Then the tumult of the armies swelled like that of the great ocean, as though it would shake the mountain of that king of the nairritas.
entries.14.8: 'Then a battle arose, thick with yakshas and rakshasas, and the rakshasa's ministers were sorely pressed in it.
entries.14.9: 'Seeing his forces in such a case, the night-ranger Dashagriva uttered many shouts of joy and rushed forward in his fury.
entries.14.10: 'And those ministers of the lord of rakshasas, of dreadful valour, each of them fought a thousand yakshas.
entries.14.11: 'Then, struck with maces and pestles, with swords, spears and javelins, Dashagriva plunged into that army.
entries.14.12: 'Struck there until he could scarcely breathe, Dashanana was hemmed in as a mountain is hemmed by clouds pouring down their torrents.
entries.14.13: 'Yet he felt no pain, though struck by the weapons of the yakshas, like a mountain drenched by a hundred streams from the clouds.
entries.14.14: 'That evil-souled one raised up his mace, which was like the staff of Kala, and entered the army, sending the yakshas to Yama's abode.
entries.14.15: 'As fire driven by the wind burns a wide thicket cluttered with dry fuel, so he burnt that army of yakshas.
entries.14.16: 'And by those great ministers, Mahodara, Shuka and the rest, the yakshas were reduced to a remnant, as clouds are by the winds.
entries.14.17: 'Some, struck and broken, fell upon the field of battle; and others in their fury bit their lips with sharp teeth in the fight.
entries.14.18: 'Worn out and clinging to one another, their weapons fallen from their hands, the yakshas sank down upon the field as riverbanks sink beneath the water.
entries.14.19: 'Between the slain going to heaven, those fighting upon the earth, and the hosts of sages looking on, there was no space left in the sky.
entries.14.20: 'Seeing those mighty lords of yakshas broken, the mighty-armed lord of wealth sent out more yakshas.
entries.14.21: 'At that moment, Rama, a yaksha named Samyodhakantaka, with wide forces and mounts, was sent and fell upon them.
entries.14.22: 'By him Maricha was struck down with a discus as though by Vishnu in battle, and fell from the mountain to the ground like a star whose merit is spent.
entries.14.23: 'But in a moment that night-ranger came to his senses, and having rested he fought that yaksha; and the yaksha, broken, fled away.
entries.14.24: 'Then Ravana entered the archway between the gates, the boundary of the doorkeepers, wonderful with gold and sprinkled with the dust of beryl.
entries.14.25: 'And as that night-ranger Dashagriva entered, king, a doorkeeper known as Suryabhanu barred his way.
entries.14.26: 'Though barred by the yaksha, the night-ranger pressed in; and when he was barred, Rama, that rakshasa would not stand still.
entries.14.27: 'Then the yaksha tore up the archway and struck him with it, and he shone as he streamed with blood, like a mountain with its running ores.
entries.14.28: 'Struck by that archway which was like a mountain peak, the hero took no hurt, because of the boon of the Self-born.
entries.14.29: 'And with that very archway he struck the yaksha in return; and the yaksha was seen no more, his body reduced to ashes.
entries.14.30: 'Then all of them fled, seeing the rakshasa's might; and afflicted with fear they entered the rivers and the caves, having cast away their weapons, worn out and pale of face.'
entries.15.1: 'Then, seeing those lords of yakshas terrified by thousands, the lord of wealth said to the great yaksha Manichara:
entries.15.2: '"Slay Ravana, lord of yakshas, that ill-conducted one of sinful mind. Be the refuge of these brave yakshas who fight so well."
entries.15.3: 'Being addressed thus, the mighty-armed Manibhadra, hard to conquer, fought surrounded by four thousand yakshas.
entries.15.4: 'Then the yakshas rushed upon the rakshasas, striking them with maces and pestles and darts, with spears and javelins and clubs.
entries.15.5: 'Making a tumultuous battle and moving as swiftly as hawks, they cried out, "Strike hard!" and "I want none of it!" and "Give way!"
entries.15.6: 'Then the gods with the gandharvas, and the sages who speak of Brahman, seeing that tumultuous battle, were filled with the greatest wonder.
entries.15.7: 'A thousand of the yakshas were slain in that battle by Prahasta, and another thousand by the peerless Mahodara.
entries.15.8: 'And by Maricha, king, enraged and eager for the fight, two thousand were struck down in the space of a moment.
entries.15.9: 'What is the yakshas' straightforward fighting, tiger among men, beside the rakshasas' reliance upon the strength of illusion? By that they were the stronger in the fight.
entries.15.10: 'Manibhadra met Dhumraksha in that great battle and, though struck in the chest with a pestle in anger, he did not waver.
entries.15.11: 'Then Manibhadra whirled his mace and struck the rakshasa Dhumraksha upon the head, and he fell reeling.
entries.15.12: 'Seeing Dhumraksha struck down and fallen, drenched in blood, Dashanana rushed upon Manibhadra in the fight.
entries.15.13: 'As Dashanana came on in fury, Manibhadra, that bull among yakshas, struck him with three spears.
entries.15.14: 'Being struck, Ravana struck at Manibhadra's crown in the battle; and by that blow of his the crown was pushed to one side.
entries.15.15: 'Yet as he fought on he stood firm and did not waver. From that day the yaksha has been known as Parshvamauli, He of the Sideways Crown. And a great roar arose upon that mountain, king.
entries.15.16: 'Then from afar the lord of wealth was seen, bearing his mace, attended by Shukra and Proshthapada and surrounded by Padma and Shankha.
entries.15.17: 'Seeing his brother in that battle, fallen from honour through a curse, that wise one spoke words worthy of the family of the Grandsire:
entries.15.18: '"When I restrained you, you did not understand, evil-minded one. Afterwards, when you have got the fruit of it and gone to hell, you will know.
entries.15.19: '"The fool who in his delusion drinks poison and does not understand — he comes to know the fruit of that deed at its ripening.
entries.15.20: '"The gods take no delight in one who is joined to dharma by nothing at all; and so you have been brought to such a state and do not understand it.
entries.15.21: '"He who slights his mother, his father and his teacher sees the fruit of it when he has come under the sway of the king of the dead.
entries.15.22: '"He who does not earn merit by penance while the body is still unsure — that fool repents afterwards, when he is dead and sees his own condition.
entries.15.23: '"From dharma come kingdom, wealth and happiness; from adharma comes only sorrow. Therefore let a man practise dharma for his happiness and cast off sin.
entries.15.24: '"The fruit of sin is sorrow, and it must be borne here by oneself. So it is only for his own destruction that a fool will do sin.
entries.15.25: '"No right understanding arises at will in one of evil mind. Fate moves everything; the one struck down is struck down by fate. As a man does his deed, so he receives its fruit.
entries.15.26: '"Wisdom, beauty, sons, courage and steadfastness — these men win in the world, gained by meritorious deeds.
entries.15.27: '"Thus you are bound for hell, you whose mind is such as this. I shall speak with you no more; with those of evil conduct the matter is settled."
entries.15.28: 'Being addressed thus by him, the rakshasa's ministers, Maricha and the rest, were struck and all fled away with their faces turned.
entries.15.29: 'Then Dashagriva was struck upon the head with a mace by that great-souled lord of yakshas, and yet was not shaken from his place.
entries.15.30: 'Then those two, Rama, striking one another in that great battle, grew neither faint nor weary, so full of wrath were they.
entries.15.31: 'The giver of wealth then loosed the fire-weapon at him; and the lord of rakshasas turned that weapon back with the weapon of Varuna.
entries.15.32: 'Then the lord of rakshasas entered into the illusion of the rakshasas, and for his enemy's destruction made a hundred thousand forms.
entries.15.33: 'A tiger, a boar, a cloud, a mountain, an ocean, a tree, a yaksha, a daitya in shape — as all of these Dashanana appeared.
entries.15.34: 'Many shapes he made, but he himself was not to be seen thereafter. Then Dashanana, Rama, took up a mighty weapon,
entries.15.35: 'and whirling his great mace he struck the giver of wealth upon the head. So struck by him, reeling and drenched in blood,
entries.15.36: 'the lord of wealth fell like an ashoka tree cut off at the root.
entries.15.37: 'Then he was surrounded there by the Treasures, Padma and the rest; and being revived by them, the giver of wealth was carried away to the Nandana grove.
entries.15.38: 'Having conquered the giver of wealth, the lord of rakshasas with a glad heart took his chariot Pushpaka, the mark of his victory —
entries.15.39: 'girt with pillars of gold, with archways of beryl and jewels, hung about with nets of pearl, bearing trees that yield every desire,
entries.15.40: 'swift as thought, going where it is wished and taking what shape is wished, moving through the sky, with steps of jewels and gold and terraces of refined gold,
entries.15.41: 'borne by the gods, imperishable, always a joy to the eye and the mind, full of marvels, wonderful in its craftsmanship, fashioned by Brahma himself,
entries.15.42: 'made with all delights, most lovely and beyond compare, neither cold nor hot, giving ease in every season, auspicious.
entries.15.43: 'Mounting that chariot that goes where it is wished, won by his valour, the king in the arrogance of his pride, evil-minded, thought the three worlds already conquered.
entries.15.44: 'Having conquered the god Vaishravana, he came down from Kailasa.
entries.15.45: 'Having won that great victory by his own splendour, the mighty night-ranger, wearing a spotless diadem and necklaces, shone seated in that finest of chariots like fire come into an assembly.'
entries.16.1: 'Having conquered his brother the giver of wealth, Rama, the lord of rakshasas went to that great reed-thicket where Mahasena was born.
entries.16.2: 'And Dashagriva saw that great golden reed-thicket, wrapped about with a web of rays like a second sun.
entries.16.3: 'Climbing that mountain with its lovely woodland glades, he saw there that the Pushpaka was held fast.
entries.16.4: 'Seeing the Pushpaka, which went where it was wished, halted and made unable to move, the lord of rakshasas considered, surrounded by his ministers:
entries.16.5: '"For what reason does this Pushpaka not go at my will? Can this be the doing of someone who stands upon the mountain?"
entries.16.6: 'Then Maricha, skilled in judgement, said, Rama, "It is not without cause, king, that the Pushpaka does not move.
entries.16.7: '"Or else this Pushpaka is the vehicle of the giver of wealth and of no other, and so it has become motionless, being parted from the lord of riches."
entries.16.8: 'While these words were passing, one came near — grim, dark and tawny, dwarfish, misshapen, shaven-headed, with drooping arms and mighty:
entries.16.9: 'Nandishvara, the attendant of Bhava, came to his side and spoke these words to the lord of rakshasas without fear:
entries.16.10: '"Turn back, Dashagriva. Shankara is sporting upon this mountain. For suparnas and nagas and yakshas, for gods and gandharvas and rakshasas,
entries.16.11: '"for all beings whatsoever this mountain has been made impassable." Hearing Nandi's words, his earrings shaking with anger
entries.16.12: 'and his eyes red with fury, Ravana came down from the Pushpaka and, saying "Who is this Shankara?", came to the foot of the mountain.
entries.16.13: 'There he saw Nandin standing not far from the god, leaning upon his blazing trident like a second Shankara.
entries.16.14: 'Seeing his monkey face, the rakshasa scorned him and let loose a great laugh there, like a cloud full of rain.
entries.16.15: 'Then the lord Nandi, angered — he who is Shankara's other body — said to that rakshasa Dashanana who stood before him:
entries.16.16: '"Since you have scorned me for my monkey shape, Dashanana, and let loose a laugh like the fall of a thunderbolt,
entries.16.17: '"therefore monkeys shall be born endowed with my shape and equal to me in valour and splendour, for the destruction of your line —
entries.16.18: '"cruel ones, whose weapons are their claws and teeth, swift as thought itself, wild in battle, swollen with strength, and ranging like moving mountains.
entries.16.19: '"They shall come together and take away this great pride of yours and your arrogance of every kind, together with your ministers and your sons.
entries.16.20: '"But what use would it be for me to slay you now, night-ranger? You are not to be slain, for you are already slain by your own deeds."
entries.16.21: 'When that great-souled god had spoken these words, the drums of the gods sounded and a rain of flowers fell from the sky.
entries.16.22: 'But that mighty one gave no thought to Nandi's words; and coming to the mountain, Dashanana said:
entries.16.23: '"Since it is for this that the Pushpaka's course has been broken as I travelled, I shall tear this mountain of yours up by the roots, lord of cattle.
entries.16.24: '"By what power does Bhava sport here always like a king? He does not know what he ought to know — that a cause of fear stands before him."
entries.16.25: 'Having spoken thus, Rama, he thrust his arms beneath the mountain and heaved at it swiftly, and the mountain shook.
entries.16.26: 'At the shaking of that mountain the god's attendants were thrown about, and Parvati too was shaken, and clung to Maheshvara.
entries.16.27: 'Then, Rama, the great god Hara, best of the gods, pressed that mountain down in play with the tip of his toe.
entries.16.28: 'And his arms, pressed beneath that mountain, were caught; and the ministers of that rakshasa stood amazed.
entries.16.29: 'Then that rakshasa, in his fury and in the crushing of his arms, let loose a cry so sudden that the three worlds were shaken by it.
entries.16.30: 'His counsellors took it for the crash of the thunderbolt at the ending of an age. The gods, with Indra at their head, were moved from their courses,
entries.16.31: 'the oceans were troubled and the mountains shook; and yakshas, vidyadharas and siddhas said, "What is this?"
entries.16.32: 'Then those ministers of his said to him as he cried out: "Propitiate the great god, the blue-throated lord of Uma.
entries.16.33: '"We see no other refuge here but him, Dashanana. Bow down with hymns of praise and go to him alone for refuge.
entries.16.34: '"Shankara is compassionate; being pleased, he will show you favour." Being addressed thus by his ministers, he praised the bull-bannered one
entries.16.35: 'with the chants of the Saman and with hymns of many kinds, and Dashanana bowed low; and a thousand years passed while the rakshasa wept.
entries.16.36: 'Then the great god, pleased, standing upon the mountain top, released his arms, Rama, and spoke these words to Dashanana:
entries.16.37: '"I am pleased with your valour and your daring, Dashanana. Since, crushed beneath the mountain, you let loose so terrible a cry —
entries.16.38: '"since by it the three worlds were made to cry out and fear came upon them, therefore you shall be known by the name Ravana, king.
entries.16.39: '"Gods and men and yakshas, and all others upon the face of the earth, shall call you thus — Ravana, who makes the worlds cry out.
entries.16.40: '"Go, son of Pulastya, and go in confidence by whatever road you please. You have my leave, lord of rakshasas; go."
entries.16.41: 'Being addressed thus by Shambhu himself, the lord of Lanka said, "If you are pleased, great god, grant me a boon, for I ask it.
entries.16.42: '"I have obtained from Brahma that I may not be slain by gods or gandharvas or danavas, by rakshasas or guhyakas or nagas, nor by any others of great strength.
entries.16.43: '"I do not count men, god; they are of small account in my eyes. And long life I have obtained from Brahma, destroyer of the three cities.
entries.16.44: '"Grant me both what remains of my life as I desire it, and a weapon." Being addressed thus by Ravana, Shankara
entries.16.45: 'gave him a great blazing sword renowned as Chandrahasa, and the remainder of his life; and then the lord of beings stood
entries.16.46: 'and, having given it, Shambhu said: "This is not to be treated with contempt by you. If it is contemned by you, it will come back to me — of that there is no doubt."
entries.16.47: 'Thus was Ravana named by Maheshvara himself; and saluting the great god he mounted the Pushpaka.
entries.16.48: 'Then Ravana ranged over the face of the earth, Rama, harrying kshatriyas of great valour here and there.
entries.16.49: 'Some, splendid and brave, kshatriyas mad for battle, would not do his bidding, and perished with all that belonged to them.
entries.16.50: 'Others, esteemed as wise and knowing that rakshasa to be hard to conquer, said to him in his pride of strength, "We are conquered."'
entries.17.1: 'Then, king, that mighty-armed one, ranging over the face of the earth, came to the forest of Himavat and wandered there.
entries.17.2: 'And there he saw a maiden wearing a black deerskin and matted hair, following the discipline of the sages, blazing like a goddess.
entries.17.3: 'Seeing that maiden endowed with beauty and holding a great vow, his soul overcome by the confusion of desire, he asked her, laughing as he spoke:
entries.17.4: '"Why do you live so, good lady, against your own youth? This treatment of such beauty as yours is not fitting.
entries.17.5: '"Your beauty is beyond compare, timid one, and maddens men with desire. It is not fitting that you should stand in penance; this is my judgement.
entries.17.6: '"Whose are you, and what is this, good lady, and who is your husband, fair-faced one? The man who enjoys you, timid one, has good fortune in this world.
entries.17.7: '"Tell me all, since I ask, and for what cause this labour of yours." Being addressed thus by Ravana, that glorious maiden replied:
entries.17.8: '"My father was Kushadhvaja, a brahmarshi of measureless splendour, the glorious son of Brihaspati, and the equal of Brihaspati in understanding.
entries.17.9: '"As that great soul was always at the recitation of the Veda, I came into being, a maiden formed of speech, and I am remembered by the name Vedavati.
entries.17.10: '"Then the gods with the gandharvas, the yakshas, rakshasas and serpents, went to my father and were eager to choose me.
entries.17.11: '"But my father did not give me to them, bull among rakshasas. I shall tell you the reason; hear it, night-ranger.
entries.17.12: '"Vishnu, lord of the gods and master of the three worlds, was my father's chosen son-in-law; therefore my father would give me to no other.
entries.17.13: '"He wished to give me to him. And hearing this, a king of the daityas named Shambhu, proud of his strength, grew wroth,
entries.17.14: '"and that sinful one killed my father as he slept at night.
entries.17.15: '"Then my mother in her wretchedness, that greatly blessed one, embraced my father's body and entered the fire.
entries.17.16: '"And I, to make true my father's wish concerning Narayana, bear him alone in my heart.
entries.17.17: '"Having taken up that vow, I practise this great austerity. All this I have told you, bull among rakshasas.
entries.17.18: '"Narayana is my husband, and no other but the best of beings. I keep this dreadful observance out of longing for Narayana. I know who you are, king; go, son of Pulastya.
entries.17.19: '"By my penance I know all that passes in the three worlds."
entries.17.20: 'Then Ravana, pierced by the arrows of Kandarpa, came down from his chariot and said again to that maiden of the great vow:
entries.17.21: '"You are full of pride, fair one, whose mind runs so. It is in the aged, doe-eyed one, that a store of merit shines.
entries.17.22: '"You are endowed with every virtue and should not speak in such a way. You are the beauty of the three worlds, timid one, and your youth is passing.
entries.17.23: '"I am the lord of Lanka, good lady, known as Dashagriva. Be my wife, and enjoy pleasures at your ease.
entries.17.24: '"And who is this whom you call Vishnu? In valour, in penance, in enjoyment and in strength —
entries.17.25: '"he is not my equal, good lady, this one whom you desire, fair-limbed one."
entries.17.26: 'When he had spoken thus, Vedavati answered him:
entries.17.27: '"Do not — do not speak so," that maiden said to the night-ranger. "Vishnu, lord of the three worlds, to whom all the worlds bow — what man of understanding but you, lord of rakshasas, would slight him?"
entries.17.28: 'Being addressed thus by Vedavati, the night-ranger then seized the maiden by the hair with the tips of his fingers.
entries.17.29: 'Then Vedavati in anger cut off that hair with her hand; her hand became a sword, and she cut the hair away.
entries.17.30: 'Blazing as though with rage and as though burning up the night-ranger, she kindled a fire and spoke, hastening to her death:
entries.17.31: '"Since I have been outraged by you, base one, I do not desire to live. Therefore, rakshasa, I shall enter the fire before your eyes.
entries.17.32: '"And since I have been outraged by you, evil-souled one, in this forest, therefore I shall be born again for your destruction.
entries.17.33: '"For a woman cannot slay a man whose purpose is sin; and if I laid a curse upon you, my penance would be spent.
entries.17.34: '"If I have done or given or offered anything at all, then may I be born of no womb, a virtuous woman, the daughter of a righteous man."
entries.17.35: 'Having spoken thus, she entered the blazing fire; and a divine rain of flowers fell from the sky on every side.
entries.17.36: 'She came into being again in a lotus, radiant as the lotus itself; and from there too she was taken again by that rakshasa as before.
entries.17.37: 'Taking that maiden bright as the heart of a lotus, he went to his own house; and having taken her, Ravana showed her to his counsellor.
entries.17.38: 'And that one who knew the marks looked at her and said to Ravana, "This fair one, if kept in the house, is seen to be for your destruction alone."
entries.17.39: 'Hearing this, Rama, Ravana cast her into the ocean; and she, coming to the earth, came into the midst of a place of sacrifice.
entries.17.40: 'Turned up by the ploughshare of a king, that virtuous one rose again. She is the daughter born to King Janaka, lord, and your wife, mighty-armed one — for you are Vishnu the eternal.
entries.17.41: 'The enemy laid low before by anger was slain by her thus, when she took refuge in your more than human valour.
entries.17.42: 'Thus that greatly blessed one is born again among mortals, in a field turned up by the ploughshare, upon the altar like a tongue of flame.
entries.17.43: 'This was she who was Vedavati of old in the Krita age; and coming to the Treta age for the destruction of that rakshasa,
entries.17.44: 'she was born in the Maithila line of the great-souled Janaka. Being born of the furrow, she is called by men Sita.'
entries.18.1: 'When Vedavati had entered the fire, Ravana mounted the Pushpaka and ranged over the earth.
entries.18.2: 'Then, coming to Ushirabija, Ravana saw King Marutta sacrificing together with the gods.
entries.18.3: 'A brahmarshi named Samvarta, the very brother of Brihaspati, that knower of dharma, was conducting the rite, surrounded by all the hosts of the gods.
entries.18.4: 'Seeing that rakshasa, hard to conquer through his boon, the gods in fear of the sight of him entered into the forms of beasts and birds.
entries.18.5: 'Indra became a peacock, the king of dharma a crow, the lord of wealth a lizard, and Varuna became a swan.
entries.18.6: 'And when the other gods too had gone in this way, destroyer of foes, Ravana entered the sacrifice like an unclean dog.
entries.18.7: 'Coming to the king, Ravana lord of rakshasas said, "Give me battle, or else say that you are conquered."
entries.18.8: 'Then King Marutta said to him, "Who are you?" And Ravana, letting loose a laugh, said:
entries.18.9: '"I am pleased with you, king, for your want of curiosity — that you do not know me, Ravana, the younger brother of the giver of wealth.
entries.18.10: '"Who else is there in the three worlds who does not know my strength, by whom my brother was conquered and this chariot taken from him?" Then King Marutta said to Ravana:
entries.18.11: '"Fortunate indeed are you, by whom an elder brother has been beaten in battle. There is none in the three worlds to be praised as you are.
