entries.30.29: '"Then, knowing the great steadfastness of that great sage and knowing his perfection in penance, I gave her to him as his wife.
entries.30.30: '"But you in your wrath, righteous one, went to that sage's hermitage and saw that woman there, blazing like a tongue of flame.
entries.30.31: '"And she was outraged by you, Shakra, stricken with desire and passion; and you were seen there in the hermitage by that great sage.
entries.30.32: '"Then you were cursed by him in his anger, one of great splendour, and by it you came, lord of the gods, to a tenth part of your former state:
entries.30.33: '"'Since my wife was outraged by you without fear, Vasava, therefore, king, you shall fall into the hand of your enemy in battle.
entries.30.34: '"'And this deed which you have begun here, evil-minded one, shall come to be among the worlds of men too — of that there is no doubt.
entries.30.35: '"'And half of it shall fall upon him who does it, and half upon you. Nor shall your station be a fixed one — of that there is no doubt.
entries.30.36: '"'And whoever shall be lord of the gods shall not be so for ever. This curse is loosed by me' — so he said to you then.
entries.30.37: '"And rebuking that wife of his, that great ascetic said, 'Ill-conducted one, be gone from the neighbourhood of my hermitage.
entries.30.38: '"'Since, endowed with beauty and youth, you did not stand fast, therefore you shall not be the only beautiful one in the world.
entries.30.39: '"'All my creatures shall have your beauty — of that there is no doubt — for it was upon that one thing that this disorder came.'
entries.30.40: '"And from that time creatures have been endowed with beauty for the most part. Then she appeased the great sage Gautama, saying,
entries.30.41: '"'I was outraged in ignorance, brahmin, by a dweller in heaven in your own form. It was not by any wish of mine, sage; you should show me favour.'
entries.30.42: '"Being addressed thus by Ahalya, Gautama answered: 'There shall be born a great warrior of the Ikshvakus, of great splendour,
entries.30.43: '"'known in the world by the name Rama, and he shall come to the forest — the mighty-armed one, Vishnu in a human body, for the sake of the brahmins. When you shall see him, good lady, then you shall be made pure.
entries.30.44: '"'For he is able to purify what wrong has been done by you. And having offered him hospitality, you shall come into my presence,
entries.30.45: '"'and then you shall dwell with me, fair one.' Having spoken thus, that sage among brahmins went to his own hermitage.
entries.30.46: '"And that wife of the speaker of Brahman performed a great penance. From the loosing of that sage's curse all this has come about.
entries.30.47: '"Remember therefore, mighty-armed one, the wrong that was done by you. By that you came into your enemy's hands, Vasava, and by nothing else.
entries.30.48: '"Perform swiftly and with full attention the Vaishnava sacrifice. Purified by that sacrifice, you shall then go to the third heaven.
entries.30.49: '"And your son, lord of the gods, was not lost in that great battle; he was taken and is safe with his grandfather in the great ocean."
entries.30.50: 'Hearing this, Mahendra performed the Vaishnava sacrifice and went up again to the third heaven, and the king of the gods ruled as before.
entries.30.51: 'This is the strength of Indrajit that I have told of; by him the lord of the gods was conquered — what then of other living beings?'
entries.30.52: 'And Rama and Lakshmana said then, "It is a marvel!" — and so did the vanaras and the rakshasas, hearing Agastya's words.
entries.30.53: 'And Vibhishana, standing at Rama's side, said, "It is a marvel; I am reminded today of what I saw long ago."
entries.30.54: 'And Rama said to Agastya, "This is the truth, and I have heard it."
entries.30.55: '"Thus, Rama, was Ravana born, that thorn in the side of the world, by whom with his son Shakra the lord of the gods was conquered in battle."
entries.31.1: Then Rama of great splendour, in wonder once again, bowed and spoke these words to Agastya, best of sages:
entries.31.2: 'Venerable one, from the time when that cruel rakshasa ranged over the earth, were the worlds empty then, best of brahmins?
entries.31.3: 'Was there then no king or man of kingly rank at all, that Ravana lord of rakshasas met with no rebuff anywhere?
entries.31.4: 'Or were the rulers of the earth stripped of their valour? Were many kings driven out and conquered by his fine weapons?'
entries.31.5: Hearing Raghava's words, the venerable sage Agastya said to Rama, smiling like the Grandsire to a lord:
entries.31.6: 'Thus harrying the kings, bull among kings, Ravana ranged over the earth, lord of the earth.
entries.31.7: 'Then he came to the city named Mahishmati, radiant as the city of heaven, where the god of the fire's seed had always his presence.
entries.31.8: 'Its king was the equal of the fire by the power of that god of the fire's seed — Arjuna by name, where the fire lies always in a bed of reeds.
entries.31.9: 'On that very day that mighty lord of the Haihayas, Arjuna, had gone to sport with his women in the waters of the Narmada.
entries.31.10: 'On that same day Ravana came there; and Ravana lord of rakshasas asked his ministers:
entries.31.11: '"Where is King Arjuna? Tell me quickly and truly. I, Ravana, have come seeking battle with that best of men. Let my coming be announced to him first."
entries.31.12: 'Being addressed thus by Ravana, those wise ministers told the lord of rakshasas that the king was not present.
entries.31.13: 'Hearing from the citizens that Arjuna had gone, the son of Vishrava went away and came to the Vindhya, that mountain like Himavat itself,
entries.31.14: 'which Ravana saw wrapped in cloud, as though the earth had risen up, as though it were scoring the sky with its peaks —
entries.31.15: 'with a thousand peaks, with lions dwelling in its caves, seeming with the waters falling from its heights to laugh like the ocean;
entries.31.16: 'with gods and danavas and gandharvas, with hosts of apsaras and kinnaras sporting there with their women, so that it was heaven itself in its great height;
entries.31.17: 'with rivers flowing over it whose water was clear as crystal, and standing like Ananta himself with his hoods and flickering tongues.
entries.31.18: 'Looking upon that Vindhya with its caves, rising like Himavat, Ravana then went to the Narmada —
entries.31.19: 'the holy river with her rolling stones and waters, flowing to the western sea,
entries.31.20: 'her pools stirred by buffaloes and wild oxen and lions, by tigers and bears and lordly elephants, scorched by the heat and thirsty;
entries.31.21: 'surrounded by chakravakas and karandavas, by swans and water-fowl, and by cranes ever in their pride and calling sweetly;
entries.31.22: 'wearing flowering trees as her ornament, with a pair of chakravakas for breasts, with broad sandbanks for hips and a line of swans for her girdle,
entries.31.23: 'her limbs anointed with the pollen of flowers, her garment the spotless foam of the water, her touch the touch of bathing, her fair eyes the opened lotuses. Coming swiftly down from the Pushpaka to the Narmada, best of rivers,
entries.31.24: 'Dashanana went down into her as into a beloved and lovely woman. And upon her fair sandbank, frequented by many sages,
entries.31.25: 'that bull among rakshasas sat with his ministers about him, and calling the Narmada a very Ganga, Ravana
entries.31.26: 'took joy at the sight of her, that lord of rakshasas, and said playfully to his ministers there, to Shuka and Sarana:
entries.31.27: '"This sun, having made the world golden with his thousand rays, giver of fierce heat, has come to the middle of the sky;
entries.31.28: '"yet knowing that I am seated here, the day-maker behaves like the moon.
entries.31.29: '"And this wind, cool from the Narmada's water, fragrant and taking away weariness, blows here in great restraint, for fear of me.
entries.31.30: '"And this best of rivers, the Narmada who swells delight, stands with her crocodiles and fishes and birds for waves like a woman in fear.
entries.31.31: '"You are wounded with the weapons of kings equal to Indra in battle, and are drenched with blood as though with the essence of sandal.
entries.31.32: '"Go down then into the Narmada, giver of peace and auspicious, like great elephants in rut with lotus-like faces going down into Ganga. Bathing in this great river you shall be rid of your sin.
entries.31.33: '"And I too today upon this sandbank, bright as the autumn moon, shall make an offering of flowers, quietly, to the wearer of matted locks."
entries.31.34: 'Being addressed thus by Ravana, Prahasta and Shuka and Sarana, with Mahodara and Dhumraksha, went down into the Narmada.
entries.31.35: 'And by those elephants of the lord of rakshasas the river Narmada was stirred, as Ganga is stirred by the great elephants Vamana and Anjana and Padma.
entries.31.36: 'Then those rakshasas of great strength, having bathed in the Narmada, came up and brought flowers for Ravana's offering.
entries.31.37: 'And upon the lovely sandbank of the Narmada, shining like a white cloud, a mountain of flowers was made in a moment by the rakshasas.
entries.31.38: 'When the flowers had been brought thus, Ravana lord of rakshasas went down into the river to bathe, like a great elephant into Ganga.
entries.31.39: 'Bathing there in due form and reciting the finest of prayers, Ravana came up out of the water of the Narmada.
entries.31.40: 'Then, casting off his wet garment and clad in white, Ravana went with joined palms, and all the rakshasas followed him,
entries.31.41: 'fallen under his sway like mountains taking form. And wherever Ravana lord of rakshasas went, there a linga of gold was carried after him.
entries.31.42: 'Setting that linga upon an altar of sand, Ravana worshipped it with perfumes and with flowers fragrant as nectar.
entries.31.43: 'Then, having worshipped that supreme one, the taker away of the sorrows of the good, the giver of boons, adorned with the moon's rays, that night-ranger sang and stretched out his arms and danced before him.'
entries.32.1: 'Not far from that place upon the Narmada's bank where the dreadful lord of rakshasas was making his offering of flowers,
entries.32.2: 'Arjuna, best of the victorious and lord of Mahishmati, was sporting with his women in the waters of the Narmada.
entries.32.3: 'And that king Arjuna, in the midst of them, shone like an elephant standing among a thousand cows.
entries.32.4: 'And wishing to test the strength of his thousand arms, he dammed the current of the Narmada, ringed about with his many arms.
entries.32.5: 'The clear water, held back by the arms of Kartavirya, came against them and rushed back upstream, sweeping away the bank.
entries.32.6: 'With its fishes and crocodiles and sea-beasts, with its litter of flowers and grass, that flood of the Narmada's waters looked like the season of rains.
entries.32.7: 'That flood, sent back as it were by Kartavirya, carried away the whole of Ravana's offering of flowers.
entries.32.8: 'Then Ravana, leaving his observance half finished, looked at the Narmada as at a beloved woman who has turned against him.
entries.32.9: 'Seeing to the west the swelling flood of the water, like a heaving of the ocean, and how it entered the eastern quarter,
entries.32.10: 'and then seeing the birds fly up in confusion, and the river standing in an unnatural stillness like a woman without expression, Ravana looked upon her.
entries.32.11: 'And with a snap of the fingers of his left hand Dashanana bade Shuka and Sarana find out the cause of that flood.
entries.32.12: 'Then those two brothers, Shuka and Sarana, at Ravana's command, went through the sky, those heroes, with their faces to the west.
entries.32.13: 'Going but half a yojana, those night-rangers saw a man sporting in the water with his women —
entries.32.14: 'like a great sala tree, his hair wet and tangled, his eyes red at the corners with wine, his splendour clouded with drink,
entries.32.15: 'damming the river with a thousand arms, that crusher of foes, as a mountain with a thousand feet might dam the earth,
entries.32.16: 'surrounded by a thousand young and lovely women, like an elephant among a thousand cows in rut.
entries.32.17: 'Seeing that most marvellous sight, the rakshasas Shuka and Sarana turned back and came to Ravana and said:
entries.32.18: '"Who is this, lord of rakshasas, like a great sala tree, who dams the Narmada as a dyke would and makes his women play?
entries.32.19: '"By that thousand of arms the river's waters are held back, and again and again she throws up surges like the heaving of the sea."
entries.32.20: 'Hearing Shuka and Sarana speak thus, Ravana said, "It is Arjuna," and went on, eager for battle.
entries.32.21: 'As Ravana lord of rakshasas turned toward Arjuna, a fierce wind blew with a roar and the dust rose;
entries.32.22: 'and once and once only the clouds sent forth a red and roaring cry. With Mahodara and Mahaparshva, Dhumraksha, Shuka and Sarana
entries.32.23: 'about him, the lord of rakshasas went to where Arjuna was; and in no long time that mighty rakshasa, dark as collyrium, came to that dreadful pool of the Narmada.
entries.32.24: 'And there the king of the rakshasas saw that lord of men, Arjuna, surrounded by women like an elephant among his cows.
entries.32.25: 'And in his fury, his eyes red, that lord of rakshasas swollen with strength
entries.32.26: 'said in a deep voice to Arjuna's ministers: "Ministers, tell the king of the Haihayas at once
entries.32.27: '"that a rakshasa named Ravana has come seeking battle." Hearing Ravana's words, those counsellors of Arjuna rose with their weapons and said to Ravana:
entries.32.28: '"The time for battle should be understood. Well said, Ravana, well said —
entries.32.29: '"but one who is eager to fight a king drunk and surrounded by his women, how can you be eager to fight Arjuna before his women, as a tiger a rutting elephant among his cows?
entries.32.30: '"Have patience today, Dashagriva, and pass the night. If you have any appetite for battle, then tomorrow, dear one, meet Arjuna in the field.
entries.32.31: '"Or if your mind is set on fighting today, filled with a thirst for battle, then slay us first and afterwards go to fight with Arjuna."
entries.32.32: 'Then those ministers of the king were destroyed in the fight by Ravana's ministers, and being hungry they devoured them.
entries.32.33: 'Then a tumult arose upon the Narmada's bank, of Arjuna's followers and of Ravana's counsellors.
entries.32.34: 'With arrows and javelins, with pikes and tridents and thunderbolt-drawing weapons, they rushed upon them from every side, tormenting Ravana's people.
entries.32.35: 'The onset of the Haihaya king's warriors was most dreadful, like the roaring of the ocean with its crocodiles and fishes and sea-beasts.
entries.32.36: 'But Ravana's ministers, Prahasta and Shuka and Sarana, in their wrath burnt up the force of Kartavirya with their splendour.
entries.32.37: 'And that deed of Ravana and his counsellors was told to Arjuna, as he sported, by the men who guarded the gates.
entries.32.38: 'Hearing it, Arjuna said to those women, "You need not fear," and came up out of that water like a dark elephant out of the waters of Ganga.
entries.32.39: 'His eyes darkened with anger, that Arjuna who was fire itself blazed up, most terrible, like the fire at the ending of an age.
entries.32.40: 'And taking up his mace with all speed, that one with fine golden armlets rushed upon the rakshasas as the sun upon the darkness.
entries.32.41: 'Raising that great mace which is wielded by the swinging of the arms, and taking the speed of Garuda, Arjuna sprang forward.
entries.32.42: 'But Prahasta, armed with his pestle, blocked his path as the Vindhya blocks the sun, standing unshakeable as the Vindhya itself.
entries.32.43: 'Then that greatly insolent Prahasta hurled his dreadful pestle bound with iron and roared like a cloud in his wrath.
entries.32.44: 'And the point of that pestle loosed from Prahasta's hand was like fire, like the crest of a blossoming ashoka, and seemed to burn as it came.
entries.32.45: 'But Arjuna, the son of Kritavirya, whose valour needed no mace, skilfully avoided that pestle as it came, mace in hand.
entries.32.46: 'Then the lord of the Haihayas rushed upon Prahasta, whirling his heavy mace, which was five hundred arms in length.
entries.32.47: 'Struck by that mace with such force, Prahasta fell like a standing mountain struck by the thunderbolt of the wielder of the bolt.
entries.32.48: 'Seeing Prahasta fallen, Maricha and Shuka and Sarana, with Mahodara and Dhumraksha, withdrew from the field.
entries.32.49: 'When his ministers had withdrawn and Prahasta was struck down, Ravana rushed swiftly upon Arjuna, best of kings.
entries.32.50: 'Then a dreadful battle began between him of the thousand arms and him of the twenty, between king and rakshasa, making the hair stand on end —
entries.32.51: 'the two like oceans in fury, like mountains torn from their roots, like two suns joined in splendour, like two fires burning,
entries.32.52: 'like two elephants swollen with strength, like two bulls over a cow, roaring like two clouds, mighty as two lions,
entries.32.53: 'wrathful as Rudra and Kala. Then those two, the rakshasa and Arjuna, struck one another hard with their maces.
entries.32.54: 'As mountains bear the dreadful strokes of the thunderbolt, so those two, the man and the rakshasa, bore there the strokes of the maces.
entries.32.55: 'As from the roar of the thunderbolt an echo is born, so from the crashing of their maces all the quarters resounded.
entries.32.56: 'Arjuna's mace, falling upon his enemy's chest, made the sky golden as lightning makes it.
entries.32.57: 'And so too the mace let fall again and again by Ravana shone upon Arjuna's chest like a meteor upon a great mountain.
entries.32.58: 'Neither Arjuna grew weary nor the lord of the hosts of rakshasas. Their fight was as the fight of Bali and Indra was of old.
entries.32.59: 'Striking one another like two bulls with their horns, like two elephants with the points of their tusks, those best of men and of rakshasas fought.
entries.32.60: 'Then Arjuna in his wrath, with all his strength, let that mace fall upon Ravana's broad chest between the breasts.
entries.32.61: 'But upon Ravana's chest, guarded by the granting of a boon, that mace broke in two as though it were weak, for all its speed, and fell to the ground.
entries.32.62: 'Yet by that fall of Arjuna's mace Ravana was driven back a bow's length and sank down groaning.
entries.32.63: 'Seeing Dashagriva reeling then, Arjuna sprang up at once and seized him, as Garuda seizes a serpent.
entries.32.64: 'And that mighty king, taking Dashanana by force with his thousand arms, bound him as Narayana bound Bali.
entries.32.65: 'As Dashagriva was being bound, the siddhas and charanas and the gods cried "Well done!" and rained flowers upon Arjuna's head.
entries.32.66: 'As a tiger takes a deer, as the lion-king takes an elephant, so the Haihaya king roared again and again for joy like a cloud.
entries.32.67: 'But Prahasta, having recovered and seeing Dashanana bound, rushed in wrath upon the king with those rakshasas.
entries.32.68: 'The onset of those night-rangers as they came shone like the rising of clouds upon the ocean at the ending of the hot season.
entries.32.69: 'Crying "Let him go, let him go!" and again "Stand, stand!", they hurled their pestles and pikes at Arjuna.
entries.32.70: 'But Arjuna, unshaken, the destroyer of foes, caught those weapons of the enemies of the gods swiftly before they reached him.
entries.32.71: 'Then with those very weapons, hard to bear and of the finest make, he pierced the rakshasas and scattered them as the wind scatters clouds.
entries.32.72: 'Having terrified the rakshasas, Kartavirya Arjuna then took Ravana and entered his city surrounded by his friends.
entries.32.73: 'Showered with flowers and unbroken grain by the brahmins and the citizens, like Puruhuta himself, Arjuna entered that city — as the thousand-eyed one entered when he had made Bali captive.'
entries.33.1: 'Then Pulastya heard, as it was told by the gods in heaven, of that taking of Ravana, which was like the taking of the wind itself.
entries.33.2: 'Then, shaken by love for his descendant, that great sage of high resolve came to see the lord of Mahishmati.
entries.33.3: 'Taking the path of the wind, that twice-born one, swift as the wind, came to the city of Mahishmati with the speed of thought itself.
entries.33.4: 'And he entered that city, thronged with glad and thriving people and resembling Amaravati, as Brahma enters Indra's Amaravati.
entries.33.5: 'He was like the sun come down to walk on foot, hard to look upon. Then the people knew him and told Arjuna.
entries.33.6: 'Knowing from their words that it was Pulastya, the king of the Haihayas set his palms together upon his head and went out to meet the ascetic.
entries.33.7: 'His household priest went before the king, taking the guest-water and the honey-offering, as Brihaspati goes before Shakra.
entries.33.8: 'Then Arjuna, seeing that sage coming like the rising sun, was awed, and bowed to him as Indra bows to the lord.
entries.33.9: 'And having offered him the honey-offering and a cow, water for the feet and the guest-water, that lord of kings said to Pulastya in a voice faltering with joy:
entries.33.10: '"Today Mahishmati has been made the equal of Amaravati, in that today I look upon you, best of brahmins, who are hard to look upon.
entries.33.11: '"Today my welfare is complete, god; today my vow is fulfilled; today my birth has borne fruit and today my penance has borne fruit, in that I bow to those feet of yours which the hosts of gods must bow to.
entries.33.12: '"This kingdom, these sons, these wives, and I myself — brahmin, what shall I do, what is to be done? Let your honour command us."
entries.33.13: 'And having asked that king after the welfare of his dharma, his fires and his sons, Pulastya said to Arjuna, king of the Haihayas:
entries.33.14: '"Lord of men with eyes like lotus-petals, with a face like the full moon — unmatched is that strength of yours by which Dashagriva was conquered by you.
entries.33.15: '"He for fear of whom the ocean and the wind stand motionless — that grandson of mine, unconquerable in battle, has been bound by you in the fray.
entries.33.16: '"My child's glory has been drunk up, and your own name proclaimed by you. Being asked now at my word, release the child Dashanana."
entries.33.17: 'Receiving Pulastya's command, Arjuna said not a word, and that lord of kings released the lord of rakshasas gladly.
entries.33.18: 'Having released that enemy of the gods, Arjuna honoured him with divine ornaments and garlands and garments, entered into a friendship without hurt in the presence of the fire, bowed to that son of Brahma, and went to his house.
entries.33.19: 'And that mighty lord of rakshasas, released by Pulastya, was embraced and given the rites of a guest, ashamed at being conquered.
entries.33.20: 'And Pulastya, the son of the Grandsire, that bull among sages, having freed Dashagriva, went to the world of Brahma.
entries.33.21: 'Thus that Ravana met with humiliation at the hands of Kartavirya, and by Pulastya's word that mighty one was released again.
entries.33.22: 'So there are stronger than the strong, delight of the Raghus. No one should be despised by a man who wishes his own good.
entries.33.23: 'Then that king of the eaters of flesh, having gained the friendship of him of the thousand arms, again made slaughter of kings and ranged over the whole earth in his pride.'
entries.34.1: 'Released by Arjuna, Ravana lord of rakshasas ranged over the whole earth, undismayed for all that had been done to him.
entries.34.2: 'Whatever rakshasa or man he heard of who was greater in strength, Ravana came upon him and challenged him proudly to battle.
entries.34.3: 'Then one day he went to the city of Kishkindha, ruled by Vali, and called Vali of the golden garland out to fight.
entries.34.4: 'Then Tara, the lord and minister of the vanaras and Tara's father, spoke to him who had come seeking the fight:
entries.34.5: '"Lord of rakshasas, Vali has gone, who would be your match. What other leaping one is able to stand before you?
entries.34.6: '"Ravana, Vali is attending the twilight rite at all four oceans, and will come within this hour; wait a little while.
entries.34.7: '"Look upon these heaps of bones, white as conches. They are of those who sought battle, king, brought down by the splendour of the lord of vanaras.
entries.34.8: '"And even if the nectar were drunk by you, rakshasa Ravana, then too, on meeting Vali, that would be the end of your life.
entries.34.9: '"Look now, son of Vishrava, upon this wonder of the world; wait this hour, and it will be hard for you to see again.
entries.34.10: '"Or if you are in haste to die, go to the southern ocean; there you shall see Vali like a fire standing upon the earth."
entries.34.11: 'Then Ravana, who makes the worlds cry out, rebuked Tara and, mounting the Pushpaka, went to the southern ocean.
entries.34.12: 'And there Ravana saw Vali, like a golden mountain with a face like the young sun, intent upon the twilight rite.
entries.34.13: 'Coming down from the Pushpaka, Ravana dark as collyrium moved with soundless steps to seize Vali quickly.
entries.34.14: 'But by chance Ravana was seen by Vali also; and seeing him with his sinful purpose, he showed no alarm.
entries.34.15: 'As a lion seeing a hare, or Garuda a serpent, so Vali gave no thought to Ravana and his sinful resolve.
entries.34.16: '"As he comes wishing to seize me, that Ravana of sinful mind — I shall tuck him under my arm and go to the three great oceans.
entries.34.17: '"They shall see my enemy under my arm, his thighs and arms and garment hanging loose — Dashagriva dangling like a serpent from Garuda."
entries.34.18: 'Having formed that resolve, Vali kept to his rite, muttering the Vedic mantras, and stood like a lord of mountains.
entries.34.19: 'And those two, the vanara and the rakshasa king, each seeking to seize the other, laboured at that work in the pride of their strength.
entries.34.20: 'But Vali, knowing by the sound of his feet that Ravana meant to lay hands on him, though his back was turned, seized him as a bird seizes a snake.
entries.34.21: 'Seizing that lord of rakshasas who wished to seize him, the monkey sprang swiftly into the sky, holding him tucked under his arm.
entries.34.22: 'And though he pressed and tore at him again and again with his nails, Vali carried Ravana off as the wind carries a cloud.
entries.34.23: 'Then Ravana's ministers, wishing to free Dashanana as he was carried away, rushed after Vali, crying out.
entries.34.24: 'Followed by them, Vali shone in the middle of the sky like the sun in the sky followed by masses of cloud.
entries.34.25: 'But those best of rakshasas, unable to overtake Vali, were left behind, worn out by the speed of his arms and thighs.
entries.34.26: 'A lord of mountains would have moved out of Vali's path as he went; how much more one who wishes to live and bears flesh and blood?
entries.34.27: 'That lord of vanaras, of great speed, where even the flights of birds do not reach, went in order to all the oceans and made his twilight salutation.
entries.34.28: 'Honoured by the beings that move through the sky, that best of sky-goers, Vali, came to the western ocean with Ravana.
entries.34.29: 'And there, having performed the twilight rite and bathed and muttered his prayer, the vanara went to the northern ocean, carrying Dashanana.
entries.34.30: 'Bearing him many thousands of yojanas, that great monkey went with his enemy like the wind and like thought itself.
entries.34.31: 'Having performed the twilight rite at the northern ocean, Vali went, carrying Dashanana, to the eastern sea.
entries.34.32: 'And there too, having performed the twilight rite, that son of Indra and lord of monkeys came back again to Kishkindha, still holding Ravana.
entries.34.33: 'Having performed the twilight rite at all four oceans, the vanara, weary with carrying Ravana, came down in the grove of Kishkindha.
entries.34.34: 'Then that best of monkeys released Ravana from under his arm and said to him, laughing again and again, "Where are you from?"
entries.34.35: 'And that lord of rakshasas, filled with great wonder, his gaze unsteady with weariness, said these words to that lord of monkeys:
entries.34.36: '"Lord of vanaras, splendid as Mahendra, I am Ravana, lord of rakshasas. I came here seeking battle, and today I have found it at your hands.
entries.34.37: '"Ah, this strength! Ah, this valour! Ah, this gravity — that I was taken up like a beast and carried round the four oceans!
entries.34.38: '"What other hero would cross the great oceans so swiftly and without weariness, hero, and carry me besides?
entries.34.39: '"Such is the going of three beings only, leaping one — of thought, of the wind and of Suparna; and of you here too, without a doubt.
entries.34.40: '"Having seen your strength, bull among monkeys, I wish for a long and loving friendship with you before the fire.
entries.34.41: '"Wives, sons, city, kingdom, enjoyment, clothing and food — let everything be held in common between us, lord of vanaras."
entries.34.42: 'Then those two, the monkey and the rakshasa, kindled the fire and, entering into brotherhood, embraced one another.
entries.34.43: 'And then those two, the monkey and the rakshasa, their arms about each other, entered Kishkindha in gladness, like two lions entering a mountain cave.
entries.34.44: 'There Ravana stayed a month, like Sugriva; and he was taken away by his ministers when they came, being eager for the destruction of the three worlds.
entries.34.45: 'Thus it happened of old, lord, that Ravana was overpowered by Vali, and made his brother in the presence of the fire.
entries.34.46: 'The strength of Vali was beyond compare and of the highest, Rama; and even he was burnt up by you as a moth by fire.'
entries.35.1: Then Rama asked that sage of the southern hermitage; and with joined palms and full of modesty he spoke these words of weight:
entries.35.2: 'Unmatched indeed was that strength of Vali and of Ravana. Yet it is my thought that these two were not the equals of Hanuman.
entries.35.3: 'Courage, skill, strength, steadiness, wisdom, and the accomplishment of policy, valour and power — all have made their dwelling in Hanuman.
entries.35.4: 'Seeing the ocean and seeing the host of monkeys sinking in despair, that mighty-armed one comforted them and leapt a hundred yojanas.
entries.35.5: 'Having entered by force the city of Lanka and Ravana's inner apartments, he saw Sita and spoke with her and comforted her.
entries.35.6: 'The leaders of the host, the sons of the ministers, the Kinkaras and Ravana's own son — all these were struck down there by Hanuman alone.
entries.35.7: 'And being freed again from his bonds and having spoken to Dashanana, he burnt Lanka to ashes as fire burns the earth.
entries.35.8: 'Of Kala, of Shakra, of Vishnu or of the lord of wealth, no such deeds are heard as those of Hanuman in battle.
entries.35.9: 'By the strength of his arms Lanka was won, and Sita and Lakshmana; and by me victory and kingdom, friends and kinsmen.
entries.35.10: 'If Hanuman had not been the friend of the lord of vanaras, who would have been able even to learn news of Janaki?
entries.35.11: 'And why, when the enmity with Vali arose, did he not burn him up like a creeper, for the sake of what pleased Sugriva?
entries.35.12: 'I think Hanuman did not know his own strength — since he saw the lord of vanaras in distress, and his life at stake.
entries.35.13: 'Tell me all this of the great-minded Hanuman, venerable one, in full and as it truly is, you who are honoured by the immortals.'
entries.35.14: Hearing Raghava's words, well reasoned, the sage then said this in Hanuman's presence:
entries.35.15: 'It is true, best of the Raghus, what you say of Hanuman. In strength there is none his equal, nor in going, nor any beyond him in mind.
entries.35.16: 'But he was cursed of old by sages with curses that do not fail; and so, being mighty and a crusher of foes, he does not know his own strength.
entries.35.17: 'And even in his childhood, Rama, the deed that was done by him, mighty one, cannot be told — it is passed over as the doing of a child.
entries.35.18: 'But if you have a mind to hear it, Raghava, compose your thought, Rama, and listen; I shall tell it.
entries.35.19: 'There is a mountain called Sumeru, whose gold was the gift of the sun, where his father, named Kesari, ruled a kingdom.
entries.35.20: 'His wife was she who is renowned as Anjana; and upon her Vayu begot an excellent son.
entries.35.21: 'Anjana bore him then, radiant as the beard of ripe rice; and she went out into the forest wishing to gather fruit.
entries.35.22: 'And he, sore afflicted by his mother's absence and by hunger, wept exceedingly, an infant like the infant born in the reed-thicket.
entries.35.23: 'Then he saw the rising sun, like a mass of hibiscus flowers; and out of greed for a fruit he sprang up toward the sun.
entries.35.24: 'Facing the young sun, that child was like the young sun in bodily form; and wishing to seize the young sun he flew up into the middle of the sky.
entries.35.25: 'As Hanuman flew thus while yet an infant, great was the wonder of the gods and danavas and yakshas:
entries.35.26: '"Not even the wind is so swift, nor Garuda, nor thought itself, as this son of Vayu going up into the highest sky.
entries.35.27: '"If the going and the valour of this child are already such, what will his speed be when he comes to youth and strength?"
entries.35.28: 'And the wind followed his own son as he flew, cool as a heap of snow, guarding him from fear of the sun's burning.
entries.35.29: 'Many thousands of yojanas he crossed, going through the sky; and by his father's strength and by his childishness he came near the sun.
entries.35.30: 'But the day-maker, thinking, "This is a child and knows no wrong," and that a purpose was bound up in it, did not burn him.
entries.35.31: 'And on the very day when he leapt to seize the sun, on that day Rahu too was seeking to seize the sun.
entries.35.32: 'By him, Rama, was Rahu brushed aside above the sun's chariot; and Rahu, the crusher of sun and moon, withdrew in terror.
entries.35.33: 'And going to Indra's dwelling in his wrath, that son of Simhika knit his brows and said to the god surrounded by the hosts of gods:
entries.35.34: '"You gave me the sun and the moon, Vasava, to take away my hunger. What is this that you have given to another, slayer of Vritra?
entries.35.35: '"Today I came at the hour of eclipse wishing to seize the sun; and another Rahu came and seized the sun at once."
entries.35.36: 'Hearing Rahu's words, Vasava rose up from his seat in agitation, wearing his golden garland.
entries.35.37: 'Then, mounting his lordly elephant, like a peak of Kailasa, four-tusked and streaming with rut, tall and bearing his ornaments, laughing with golden bells,
entries.35.38: 'Indra set Rahu before him and went to where the sun was, and Hanuman with him.
entries.35.39: 'Then Rahu came on with great haste, leaving Vasava behind; and he was seen by Hanuman rushing on like a mountain peak.
entries.35.40: 'Then, leaving the sun and looking on Rahu as a fruit, he sprang up again into the sky to seize the son of Simhika.
entries.35.41: 'And leaving the sun, Rama, the leaping one rushed at him; and Rahu, seeing this, turned back with his face away, and only his head remained toward him.
entries.35.42: 'And looking to Indra for a protector, the son of Simhika cried out again and again in his terror, "Indra! Indra!"
entries.35.43: 'Hearing that voice of Rahu crying out, which was known to him beforehand, Indra said, "Do not fear; I shall destroy him."
entries.35.44: 'Then, seeing Airavata and thinking, "Here is a great fruit indeed," the son of Maruta rushed upon the king of elephants.
entries.35.45: 'And as he rushed on wishing to seize Airavata, his form for a moment was terrible and blazing as of Indra and Agni together.
entries.35.46: 'And as he came on thus, the lord of Shachi, not greatly angered, struck him with the thunderbolt loosed from his hand.
entries.35.47: 'Then he fell upon a mountain, struck by Indra's bolt; and as he fell his left jaw was broken.
entries.35.48: 'And when that child fell, reeling from the stroke of the bolt, the wind grew wroth with Indra, to the hurt of all creatures.
entries.35.49: 'That lord who moves within creatures gathered up his going and entered a cave, taking his own infant son with him.
entries.35.50: 'Shutting up the passages of dung and urine in creatures, causing the greatest anguish, he held back all beings as Vasava holds back the rains.
entries.35.51: 'By the wrath of the wind, creatures everywhere were left without breath, and with their joints breaking apart they became as wood.
entries.35.52: 'Without recitation of the Veda or the cry of Vashat, without rite and bereft of dharma, the three worlds through the wind's wrath became as though set in hell.
entries.35.53: 'Then creatures with the gandharvas, with gods and asuras and men, ran to Prajapati in their distress, desiring ease.
entries.35.54: 'The gods, their bellies grown huge, said with joined palms: "By you, lord of creatures, were the four kinds of beings created;
entries.35.55: '"and by you was the wind given us as the lord of our life. Why then has he today, best of beings, being the lord of our breath,
entries.35.56: '"held us back and made us suffer, as women are shut up in an inner chamber? For that we have come to you for refuge, struck down by the wind."
entries.35.57: 'Hearing this of his creatures, Prajapati the lord of creatures said, "There is a cause," and spoke to them again:
entries.35.58: '"Hear, creatures, the whole cause for which the wind grew angry and held you back; it should be heard, and it is fit for you to hear.
entries.35.59: '"His son was struck down today by Indra, lord of the immortals, at Rahu's word; and thereupon the wind was enraged.
entries.35.60: '"Bodiless, the wind moves within bodies, protecting them; without the wind the body is no better than wood.
entries.35.61: '"The wind is breath, the wind is happiness, the wind is all this world; and abandoned by the wind, the world finds no happiness.
entries.35.62: '"And this very day the world, whose life is the wind, has been abandoned by him; this very day you stand breathless, like wood or like walls.
entries.35.63: '"Let us go therefore to where the Maruta is, who is the giver of our ease. Let us not go to destruction without appeasing him, sons of Aditi."
entries.35.64: 'Then Prajapati, together with his creatures and with the gods, gandharvas, serpents and guhyakas, went to where the wind sat, holding his son who had been struck by the lord of the gods.
entries.35.65: 'And the four-faced one, seeing that son in the lap of the ever-moving one, radiant as the sun and as fire and as gold, then showed him compassion, together with the gods and gandharvas, sages, yakshas and rakshasas.'
entries.36.1: 'Then the wind, tormented by his son's slaying, seeing the Grandsire, took up that infant and rose before the Creator.
entries.36.2: 'With his earrings and crown and garland swaying and his golden ornaments, the wind fell at his feet and stood before the Ordainer.
entries.36.3: 'And that knower of the Veda, resplendent with his hanging ornaments, raised the wind up with his hand and stroked that infant.
entries.36.4: 'At the mere touch of the lotus-born one, given in play, that child came to life again like a crop watered with rain.
entries.36.5: 'Seeing him living, the bearer of fragrance, who is breath itself, moved gladly among all creatures as before, when he had held himself back.
entries.36.6: 'And those creatures, released from the wind's withholding, grew glad, as lotus-pools with their lotuses when freed from cold and burning.
entries.36.7: 'Then Brahma, of the three pairs, of the three peaks and the three abodes, honoured by the gods, spoke to the deities, wishing to please the Maruta:
entries.36.8: '"Mahendra, Isha, Varuna, lord of creatures, lord of wealth — though you know all this, I shall speak; hear what is for your good.
entries.36.9: '"There will be a task to be done for you by this child. Speak therefore, all of you, and grant boons for the Maruta's contentment."
entries.36.10: 'Then the thousand-eyed one, filled with affection and fair of face, raised up a garland of lotuses and said:
entries.36.11: '"Since his jaw was struck by the thunderbolt loosed from my hand, this tiger among monkeys shall bear the name Hanuman.
entries.36.12: '"And I shall grant him a boon that is supreme and wonderful: from this day he shall not be slain by my thunderbolt."
entries.36.13: 'Then Martanda, the venerable dispeller of darkness, said, "I give him a hundredth part of my own splendour.
entries.36.14: '"And when he has the power to study the sciences, then I shall give him that learning by which he shall be eloquent.
entries.36.15: '"And there shall be none his equal in the understanding of the sciences." And Varuna gave a boon: "There shall be no death for him even in a hundred thousand years, from my noose or from water."
entries.36.16: 'And Yama said: "I grant, being pleased, that he shall not be slain by my staff, and that he shall be free of sickness always, and shall know no despondency in battle.
entries.36.17: '"This mace of mine shall not slay him in any encounter." So spoke the giver of boons, the one with the tawny eye.
entries.36.18: '"He shall not be slain by me or by my weapons." Such was the supreme boon given him by Shankara too.
entries.36.19: '"He shall not be slain by any of the staffs of Brahma; he shall be long of life and great of soul" — so said Brahma.
entries.36.20: 'And Vishvakarma, seeing that child like the young sun, that best and greatest-minded of craftsmen gave him a boon:
entries.36.21: '"By those divine weapons that are made by me in battle he shall not be slain, and he shall be long of life."
entries.36.22: 'Then the four-faced one, seeing him adorned with the boons of the gods, that teacher of the world said with a pleased heart to the wind:
entries.36.23: '"A terror to his enemies and a giver of safety to his friends, unconquerable shall your son be, Maruta, this son of the wind.
entries.36.24: '"Taking what form he wishes and going where he wishes, swift as desire, best of the leaping ones, his course shall be unhindered and he shall be renowned.
entries.36.25: '"He shall do deeds in battle that make the hair stand on end, for the destruction of Ravana and for the pleasure of Rama."
entries.36.26: 'Having spoken thus and taken leave of the Maruta, all of them with the Grandsire at their head went as they had come.
entries.36.27: 'And the bearer of fragrance took his son and brought him home, and going forth he told Anjana of the boons that had been given.
entries.36.28: 'Having won those boons, Rama, and endowed with the gift of them, he was filled with the strength that dwelt in him as the ocean is filled.
entries.36.29: 'But even as that bull among monkeys was thus swelling with power, he began to offend without fear in the hermitages of the great sages.
entries.36.30: 'The ladles and vessels, the fire-offerings, the stores of bark and hide — these he broke and tore and scattered, though those sages were peaceable.
entries.36.31: 'Such were the deeds that mighty one took to doing, having been made by Shambhu proof against every staff of Brahma.
entries.36.32: 'The sages knew him, and bore with him according to their power.
entries.36.33: 'Though forbidden by Kesari and by the wind, that son of Anjana, that vanara, still overstepped all bounds.
entries.36.34: 'Then the great sages born in the lines of Bhrigu and Angiras, best of the Raghus, cursed him — not in great anger, nor in great indignation:
entries.36.35: '"Since, leaning upon that strength, you trouble us, leaping one, therefore for a long time you shall not know it, being confused by our curse. When your glory is called to mind, then your strength shall grow."
entries.36.36: 'Then, his splendour and vigour taken from him by the power of the sages' word, he went about those hermitages grown gentle.
entries.36.37: 'Now Riksharajas by name, the father of Vali and Sugriva, was king of all the vanaras, radiant as the sun in splendour.
entries.36.38: 'And that lord of monkeys, having ruled the vanaras a long while, that Riksharajas came at length to the law of time.
entries.36.39: 'And when he had set, Vali was placed by ministers skilled in counsel in his father's station, and Sugriva in Vali's.
entries.36.40: 'And between him and Sugriva there was from childhood a friendship undivided and without flaw, like the friendship of the wind with fire.
entries.36.41: 'By the power of that curse alone he did not know his own strength; and when the enmity between Vali and Sugriva arose, Rama —
entries.36.42: 'for indeed, Rama, this Sugriva was driven about by Vali,
entries.36.43: 'yet the son of Maruta did not know the strength within himself, god; that best of monkeys had his strength taken away by the sages' curse,
entries.36.44: 'like a lion hemmed in by elephants, standing yet ready in the fight.
entries.36.45: 'In valour and energy, in understanding and might, in good conduct and sweetness, in policy and its opposite, in gravity and skill, in high courage and steadiness — who in the world is greater than Hanuman?
entries.36.46: 'And that lord of monkeys, wishing to learn grammar and eager to ask his questions, went facing the sun from the mountain of sunrise to the mountain of setting, bearing that great text, he who cannot be measured.
entries.36.47: 'That lord of monkeys will master it with its rules and commentary, its senses and its words, its great meanings and its digest. For there is none his equal in learning, nor in mastery of the metres and their movement.
entries.36.48: 'In all the sciences and in the practice of penance he vies indeed with the teacher of the gods. This knower of the meaning of the nine grammars shall be a Brahma, and by your favour.
entries.36.49: 'Who shall stand before Hanuman — before the ocean as it would break forth, before the fire as it would burn up the worlds at the ending of an age, before Antaka himself?
entries.36.50: 'He and the other great lords of monkeys — Sugriva, Mainda and Dvivida, Nila, Tara and Tara's son and Nala and Rambha — were all created by the gods for your sake, Rama.
entries.36.51: 'So all is told that you asked of me; this deed of Hanuman in his childhood I have told.'
entries.36.52: Hearing what Agastya told, Rama and Sumitra's son and the vanaras with the rakshasas were filled with the highest wonder.
entries.36.53: And Agastya said to Rama, 'All this you have heard. We have seen you and spoken with you; Rama, we shall now go.'
entries.36.54: Hearing these words of Agastya of fierce splendour, Raghava with joined palms bowed and said to the great sage:
entries.36.55: 'Today my gods are pleased, and my fathers and forefathers; by the mere sight of you they are ever contented, with all their kin.
entries.36.56: 'But this must be made known by me, which I say with longing; and it should be done by you for my sake, out of compassion.
entries.36.57: 'Having settled the people of the city and the country in their own affairs, I have come; and I shall perform sacrifices by the power of you who are good.
entries.36.58: 'You shall always be the officiants at my sacrifices; you of great valour, who desire to show me favour.
entries.36.59: 'Leaning upon you, whose sins are burnt away by penance, I shall be blessed by my fathers and shall be wholly content.
entries.36.60: 'You should therefore come here without fail, together.' And Agastya and the sages of firm vows, hearing that,
entries.36.61: 'said to him, "So be it," and made ready to depart.
entries.36.62: Having spoken thus, all those sages went as they had come; and Raghava pondered upon that same matter in wonder.
entries.36.63: Then, when the sun had set, dismissing the kings and the vanaras and performing the twilight rite in due form, that best of men, when night had come on, went within his inner apartments.
entries.37.1: When Kakutstha had been consecrated in dharma and was known for what he was, that first night passed, which swelled the joy of the citizens.
entries.37.2: When that night was over, at dawn the bards who wake the king, gentle men, took their places in the royal house.
entries.37.3: All of them full-throated and trained like kinnaras, they praised that heroic king in due form, filled with gladness:
entries.37.4: 'Awake, gentle hero, increaser of Kausalya's joy. For the whole world sleeps while you sleep, lord of men.
entries.37.5: 'Your valour is as Vishnu's and your beauty as the Ashvins'; in understanding you are the equal of Brihaspati and the peer of Prajapati.
entries.37.6: 'Your patience is like the earth's, in splendour you are like the sun; your speed is like the wind's and your gravity like the ocean's.
entries.37.7: 'You are unshakeable as Sthanu, and such is your gentleness as the moon's. There have been no such kings before, lord of men,
entries.37.8: 'as you, unassailable, constant in dharma and devoted to your people's good. Glory does not leave you, nor Fortune, bull among men.
entries.37.9: 'Shri and Dharma are both established in you always, Kakutstha.' These and other sweet things were recited by the bards.
entries.37.10: And the sutas woke Raghava with divine hymns of praise; and being praised with those praises, Raghava awoke.
entries.37.11: He left that couch spread with white coverings and rose as Hari Narayana rises from his serpent bed.
entries.37.12: And as that great one rose, men bowed low with joined palms and brought him water in bright vessels by the thousand.
entries.37.13: Having made himself pure with water and offered the oblation into the fire at its hour, he went swiftly to the holy shrine served by the Ikshvakus.
entries.37.14: There, having worshipped the gods and the fathers and the brahmins in due form, Rama came out into the outer court surrounded by his people.
entries.37.15: The great-souled ministers with the household priests, Vasishtha and the rest, attended him, blazing like fires.
entries.37.16: And great-souled kshatriyas, lords of many lands, sat at Rama's side as the immortals at Shakra's.
entries.37.17: And Bharata and Lakshmana were there, and the renowned Shatrughna, and they waited upon him gladly like the three Vedas upon a sacrifice.
entries.37.18: The attendants went with joined palms and glad faces, and many stood at his side and sat down, well pleased.
entries.37.19: And twenty vanaras of great valour, taking what form they wished, Sugriva at their head, of great might, waited upon Rama.
entries.37.20: And Vibhishana, surrounded by four rakshasas, waited upon that great one as the guhyakas upon the lord of wealth.
entries.37.21: And elders learned in scripture and men of good family, discerning, bowed with their heads to the king and waited upon him.
entries.37.22: Thus surrounded, the king, encircled by glorious sages, by kings of great valour and by vanaras with the rakshasas,
entries.37.23: shone as the lord of the gods is ever waited upon by the sages; and in that aspect he shone even beyond the thousand-eyed one.
entries.37.24: And as they sat there, many sweet stories joined with dharma were told by great-souled men who knew the ancient tales.
entries.38.1: So the mighty-armed Raghava sat day after day, ordering all affairs among the people of the city and the country.
entries.38.2: Then after some days Raghava, with joined palms, spoke these words to the Vaideha, lord of Mithila:
entries.38.3: 'You are our sure refuge, and by you we have been protected. By the fierce power of your splendour Ravana was slain by me.
entries.38.4: 'Between all the Ikshvakus and all the Maithilas there is joy beyond compare, king, with our kinship at its head.
entries.38.5: 'Let your honour go now to your own city, taking these jewels with you, king; and Bharata will follow behind you for your help.'
entries.38.6: And the king said, 'So be it,' and spoke to Raghava: 'I am pleased with you, king, with your presence and your good conduct.
entries.38.7: 'And these jewels which have been gathered for my sake — all of these, king, I give to my daughter.'
entries.38.8: Having spoken thus to Kakutstha, the glorious Janaka with a glad heart took leave of Raghava and went to Mithila.
entries.38.9: Then, when Janaka had gone, the lord Raghava with joined palms spoke these words to his uncle, the king of the Kekayas:
entries.38.10: 'This kingdom, and I myself, and Bharata with Lakshmana, all depend upon you, king; and you are our refuge, bull among men.
entries.38.11: 'For the king is old and will grieve for your sake. Therefore it seems best that you should go this very day, lord of earth.
entries.38.12: 'You shall be followed by Lakshmana as your escort, taking abundant wealth and jewels of many kinds.'
entries.38.13: And Yudhajit said, 'So be it,' to Raghava concerning his going, and 'Let the jewels and the wealth be yours and unfailing.'
entries.38.14: And that increaser of the Kekayas went round the king from left to right, having first been saluted and gone round by Rama.
entries.38.15: And the lord of the Kekayas set out with Lakshmana as his companion, as Vasava set out with Vishnu when the asura Vritra had been slain.
entries.38.16: Then, having dismissed him, Rama embraced his fearless friend Pratardana, lord of Kashi, and said:
entries.38.17: 'You have shown your affection and shown the highest friendship; and effort was made by you together with Bharata, king.
entries.38.18: 'Let your honour go therefore today, lord of Kashi, to the city of Varanasi — lovely, guarded by you, bright and fair of gateways.'
entries.38.19: Having said only this, Kakutstha rose from his high seat and, that soul of dharma, embraced him closely to his breast.
entries.38.20: Then that increaser of Kausalya's joy dismissed him; and being given leave by Raghava, the fearless lord of Kashi went swiftly to Varanasi.
entries.38.21: Having dismissed the lord of Kashi, Raghava said to the three hundred lords of earth, with a smile, in sweet-sounding words:
entries.38.22: 'Your affection has been unwavering and guarded by your splendour; and dharma has been constant in you always, and truth always.
entries.38.23: 'By your influence and by the splendour of you great-souled ones, that evil-souled and evil-minded Ravana, basest of rakshasas, was slain.
entries.38.24: 'I was but the instrument there; Ravana was slain by your splendour in the fight, with his hosts, his sons, his ministers and his kinsmen.
entries.38.25: 'And you were brought together by the great-souled Bharata, when he heard that King Janaka's daughter had been carried off from the forest.
entries.38.26: 'A very long time has passed for all you great-souled kings, who have been ready for so long; so I think it well that you should go.'
entries.38.27: And those kings, filled with great joy, answered him: 'By good fortune you are victorious, Rama, and established in your own kingdom.
entries.38.28: 'By good fortune Sita has been brought back, by good fortune the enemy has been beaten. This is our highest desire and this our greatest joy —
entries.38.29: 'that we should see you victorious, Rama, with your enemies destroyed.
entries.38.30: 'And it befits you that you should praise us so; but we do not know how to speak such praise, you who deserve all praise.
entries.38.31: 'We take our leave and shall go; you are always in our hearts. We live, mighty-armed one, filled with great affection in this; and may your affection for us be constant, great king.'
entries.38.32: 'So be it,' said the kings, filled with the highest joy; and all of them said this to Raghava with joined palms, eager to go.
entries.38.33: And being honoured by Rama, they went each to his own country.
entries.39.1: Those great-souled kings went joyfully, making the earth shake with their thousands of elephants and horses.
entries.39.2: For there were many divisions gathered there for Raghava's sake, at Bharata's command, glad with their forces and their mounts.
entries.39.3: And those lords of earth, filled with pride in their strength, said, 'We did not see Rama and Ravana standing before us in the fight.
entries.39.4: 'We were gathered together by Bharata afterwards to no purpose. For the rakshasas would surely have been swiftly slain by us kings.
entries.39.5: 'Guarded by the strength of Rama's arms and of Lakshmana's, we would have fought at ease beyond the sea and without fever.'
entries.39.6: These and a thousand other tales those kings told there as they went to their own kingdoms, filled with gladness —
entries.39.7: to their own chief kingdoms, prosperous and glad, rich in wealth and grain, full and abounding in treasure.
entries.39.8: And having gone as of old, those kings gave jewels of many kinds as gifts, to do what would please Rama —
entries.39.9: horses and carriages and jewels, elephants wild with rut, the finest sandalwood and divine ornaments,
entries.39.10: gems, pearls and coral, and handmaids endowed with beauty; and they gave goats and sheep of many kinds and chariots of many kinds.
entries.39.11: And Bharata and Lakshmana and the mighty Shatrughna took those jewels and came again to their own city.
entries.39.12: And coming to lovely Ayodhya, those bulls among men brought those wonderful jewels to Rama.
entries.39.13: And Rama, receiving all of it with affection, that great one gave it to King Sugriva, who had done what was to be done;
entries.39.14: and Raghava gave to Vibhishana too and to the others as well, to the rakshasas and monkeys by whom he was surrounded when he won the victory.
entries.39.15: And all those monkeys and rakshasas of great strength bore upon their heads and upon their arms the jewels Rama had given.
entries.39.16: And that great warrior, king of the Ikshvakus, taking Hanuman and the mighty-armed Angada upon his lap,
entries.39.17: Rama with eyes like lotus-petals said to Sugriva: 'This Angada is your good son, and this son of the wind your minister.
entries.39.18: 'Both are fit for Sugriva's counsel and devoted to my good. They deserve honour of many kinds at your hands, lord of monkeys.'
entries.39.19: Having spoken thus, that renowned one took the ornaments from his own limbs and bound those costly things upon Angada and Hanuman.
entries.39.20: And addressing those bulls among the troop-leaders of great valour — Nila, Nala, Kesari, Kumuda and Gandhamadana,
entries.39.21: Sushena and the hero Panasa, Mainda and Dvivida, Jambavan and Gavaksha, Vinata and Dhumra,
entries.39.22: Valimukha and Prajangha, and the mighty Sannada, Darimukha, Dadhimukha and the troop-leader Indrajanu —
entries.39.23: sweetly and in gentle words, as though drinking them in with his eyes, he said: 'You are my friends, and my very body, and my brothers.
entries.39.24: 'By you I was raised out of calamity, dwellers in the woods; and King Sugriva is fortunate in you, best of friends.'
entries.39.25: Having spoken thus, he gave them ornaments as each deserved, and precious diamonds, and that bull among men embraced them.
entries.39.26: And they, tawny as honey, drank fragrant meads and ate well-dressed flesh and roots and fruits.
entries.39.27: Thus a full month and more passed for them as they dwelt there; yet in their devotion to Rama they all thought it a moment.
entries.39.28: And Rama too took his pleasure with those vanaras who take what form they wish, and with the rakshasas of great valour and the mighty bears.
entries.39.29: Thus a second month, the cool season, passed for them in ease — for the glad vanaras and for the rakshasas in every way,
entries.39.30: dwelling in the lovely city of the Ikshvakus in the highest content; and by Rama's doing of what pleased them, their time passed happily.
entries.40.1: While those bears and vanaras and rakshasas were dwelling thus, Raghava of great splendour said to Sugriva:
entries.40.2: 'Go, gentle one, to Kishkindha, which even gods and asuras cannot assail, and rule with your ministers that kingdom which has no thorn in it.
entries.40.3: 'And look with the highest affection upon Angada, mighty-armed one, and upon Hanuman and upon Nala of great strength;
entries.40.4: 'upon your father-in-law the hero Sushena, and upon Tara best of the strong, upon the unassailable Kumuda and upon Nila of great strength;
entries.40.5: 'upon the hero Shatabali, and upon Mainda and Dvivida, upon Gaja, Gavaksha, Gavaya and the mighty Sharabha; and look with affection upon Gandhamadana too;
entries.40.6: 'upon Rishabha of great valour and upon the mighty Jambavan — and upon all these great-souled ones who gave up their lives for my sake.
entries.40.7: 'Look upon them with affection, and do nothing that displeases them.'
entries.40.8: Having spoken thus to Sugriva and embraced him again and again, Rama then said to Vibhishana in sweet words:
entries.40.9: 'Rule Lanka in dharma; you are held by me to be a knower of dharma. You are esteemed by the city and by the rakshasas and by your own brother.
entries.40.10: 'And do not set your mind upon unrighteousness in any way, king. For kings who are wise enjoy the earth for long.
entries.40.11: 'And I am always to be remembered by you with the highest affection, king, together with Sugriva. Go now, free of fever.'
entries.40.12: Hearing Rama's words, the bears and vanaras and rakshasas praised Kakutstha again and again, crying, 'Well said, well said!'
entries.40.13: 'Your understanding, mighty-armed one, and your valour are wonderful; and your sweetness, Rama, is always supreme, as of the Self-born himself.'
entries.40.14: As the vanaras and rakshasas were speaking thus, Hanuman bowed low and said these words to Raghava:
entries.40.15: 'Let my love for you stand always, king; and let my devotion be constant, hero, and let my heart go nowhere else.
entries.40.16: 'So long, hero, as the story of Rama shall walk upon the face of the earth, so long shall the breath dwell in my body; of that there is no doubt.
entries.40.17: 'And that divine deed of yours and that story of you, delight of the Raghus — let the apsaras recite it to me, bull among men.
entries.40.18: 'Hearing that nectar of your acts, hero and lord, I shall carry away my longing as the wind carries away a line of cloud.'
entries.40.19: And as Hanuman spoke thus, Rama rose from his fine seat and embraced him in affection and said these words:
entries.40.20: 'It shall be so, best of monkeys; there is no doubt of it. So long as this story of mine shall walk in the world, so long shall your glory endure, and the breath in your body too.
entries.40.21: 'For so long as the worlds shall stand, so long shall my story stand.
entries.40.22: 'For each single service of yours I would give my life, monkey; but a man becomes fit to repay a kindness only when calamity comes upon the giver.'
entries.40.23: Then Raghava loosed from his neck a necklace bright as the moon, sparkling with beryl, and bound it upon Hanuman's neck.
entries.40.24: And with that great necklace bound upon his breast, that monkey shone like a golden lord of mountains with the moon upon its crest.
entries.40.25: Hearing this of Raghava, the vanaras rose one after another and, bowing their heads to his feet, went out, those mighty ones.
entries.40.26: And Sugriva, held close to Rama's breast, and the righteous Vibhishana — all of them were overcome with tears.
entries.40.27: And all of them, choked with weeping, their eyes full of tears and their senses gone, as though stupefied with sorrow, left Raghava then.
entries.40.28: Having been shown such favour by the great-souled Raghava, they all went each to his own house, as the embodied soul leaves the body.
entries.40.29: Then those rakshasas and bears and vanaras, having bowed to Rama who increases the line of the Raghus, their eyes filled with the tears of parting, went back each to his own dwelling.
